paper_title: K2-Horizon: A Frontier Fleet of Open Source Language Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We present K2-Horizon, a fleet of six fully open language models, from a 0.9B dense model to a 375B-A23B MoE, built for general-purpose reasoning and agentic work across math and science, software engineering, deep research, office automation, and beyond. The models lead or are competitive with strong open models of their size on agentic and coding benchmarks. On the modeling side, to strengthen reasoning, we introduce Mixture-of-Value Attention (MoVA), applying MoE to attention value projections, and softplus attention gating, a more flexible, theoretically motivated gate. Our 36B-A4B model uses both and nearly matches a 32B dense model trained on the same data, with one-seventh the active parameters. We also introduce Uno, lossless diffusion adapters that speed up decoding by up to 2.2x without a separate draft model. Our release follows the LLM360 definition of open source for transparency and reproducibility: the full development history, including intermediate checkpoints from every training stage, pre-training data, training logs, and all training, evaluation, and infrastructure code, notably our production-scale xLLM framework for dense and MoE training and the RL360 reinforcement-learning stack. Beyond the data itself, we release and document in detail every pipeline that built it, the part of model development that open releases most rarely disclose. These pipelines produced roughly 10T synthetic pre-training tokens, showing that synthetic data can be a major ingredient of pre-training at scale. Four of the models share one 22T-token pre-training corpus and recipe, revealing consistent scaling behavior and enabling controlled studies of scale and sparsity. All artifacts are available at https://ifm.ai/k2/

1 Introduction
We present K2-Horizon, a fleet of six fully open language models designed for agentic tasks. While many
capable open-weight models are available, the data, intermediate states, and decisions behind them are
rarely released. K2-Horizon succeeds K2-V2 (K2 Team, Institute of Foundation Models, 2025) in the
LLM360 family. It extends that fully open approach from a single base model to the complete development
lifecycle of six models: pre-training, mid-training, post-training, and deployment. The family ranges from
a 0.9B dense model for on-device use to a 375B mixture-of-experts flagship that activates 23B parameters
per token, and achieves competitive performance on general-purpose reasoning and agentic tasks, such as
math and science, software engineering, deep research, file manipulation, customer service, and tool calling.
sections.content: For all six models, we release the final weights, intermediate checkpoints from every training stage, quantized builds, training logs, the training data, and the code used throughout the training and evaluation pipeline. This code includes our training framework (xLLM), RL stack (RL360), and evaluation harness (Eval360). All released artifacts are documented in the Released Artifacts section. Four of the models (3.7B, 7B, 32B, and 36B-A4B) were pre-trained on the same 22T-token corpus with the same recipe, including two pairs trained on identical data batches. The release provides complete, transparent recipe for reproducing frontier models at various sizes, allows controlled comparisons across scale and between dense and sparse architectures, and supports studies of how each ingredient influences the final model. The family covers the main deployment settings  (Table 1)  . The 0.9B targets phones and other memoryconstrained devices. The 3.7B and 7B models are designed for local assistants and coding tools on consumer hardware, and serve as accessible platforms for fine-tuning and reinforcement-learning research. The 32B and 36B-A4B target self-hosted technical and agentic assistants, and the 375B-A23B targets multi-GPU server deployment. When compared against four open-weight models released around the same time (GLM-5.2, MiniMax M3, Nemotron 3 Ultra, and Inkling), our 375B-A23B is smaller than most of them in both active and total parameters, yet ranks first or second on most agentic and coding benchmarks (see the overview figure on the first page). It leads all four on Toolathlon-Verified (65.3), where it also surpasses GPT-5.6 Terra and comes close to GPT-5.6 Luna. It also leads them on repository-level code understanding without internet access (SWE-Atlas-QnA, 48.4), and it exceeds both GPT-5.6 variants on τ 3-Banking. Its main gap is expert-level scientific reasoning (HLE and CritPt; 7.2). The 36B-A4B matches or stays within few points of our own dense 32B (seven times its active parameters), trained on the same data, on every benchmark (7.3). Among small models, the 7B outperforms similarly sized open-weight models on most benchmarks, and both the 7B and 3.7B lead SWE-bench Verified by wide margins (7.4). Our main contributions are: Architecture. Grouped RMSNorm across the family, and Mixture-of-Value Attention (MoVA) with softplus attention gate in the 36B-A4B (2). Pre-training and mid-training. production-scale test of the scaling-collapse approach of Bergsma et al. (2026): four models that span dense and sparse architectures and nearly an order of magnitude in size, trained on 22T tokens with hyperparameters scaled together, follow nearly identical normalized loss curves. Pre-training, mid-training, and context extension all run on xLLM (3.2.2), our opensource training infrastructure, which supports both dense and MoE models at production scale (3, 3.3.2). Data. About 10T synthetic pre-training tokens in web-heavy mix chosen by benchmark scores predicted at production scale (4), and agentic trajectories introduced from the start of context extension rather than only in post-training (5). 5 Post-training. For the 375B-A23B, reinforcement learning of separate domain experts for search, knowledge work, tool use, scientific reasoning, and instruction following with abstention, merged into one model by weight merging and refined with targeted supervised fine-tuning (6.3, 6.4); the other models follow adapted versions of this pipeline (1.1). Inference. Uno, lossless diffusion adapters distilled from each model that speed up decoding by up to 2.2 without separate draft model (9, 10). 1.1 walks through the development lifecycle and serves as guide to the rest of the report.

sections.title:
1.1 Model Development Lifecycle
Developing a large language model involves a sequence of training stages, each starting from the checkpoint
produced by the previous one. We describe the sequence for the 375B flagship; the other models follow
it with minor differences noted in later sections. Figure 1 shows the training timeline for all six models,
including pre-training and mid-training for the 32B and 36B-A4B models.
sections.content: Pre-training. Pre-training gives the model most of its knowledge and its general language ability: starting from initialization, the model is trained to predict the next token on 8k-token sequences of web text, code, mathematics, scientific literature, and multilingual data, about 10T tokens of which are synthetic (4). This stage accounts for most of the compute, so its key decisions are made in advance through small-scale experiments. Learning rates follow scaling rule fitted across model sizes (3.1), and the data mix is chosen by its benchmark scores predicted at the production scale rather than measured in small ablations, which led us to web-heavy mix (4.9). The flagship is trained on 15.1T tokens in two phases, the second with an updated data mix, while the dense and MoVA models see 22T tokens. All runs except the 0.9B hold constant learning rate to the end, and the decay is instead realized by averaging the final checkpoints before mid-training. Mid-training. Mid-training continues the same objective on about 1.9T tokens of more carefully curated data in four stages, extending the context window from 32k tokens in stage 1 to 128k in stage 2 and 512k in stages 3 and 4, with the RoPE base raised alongside (3.1.3). Most of the budget goes to stage 1, during which the learning rate also decays to 10% of its peak. The data shift toward the capabilities the final model needs: long documents, reasoning, coding, and instruction following, together with agent trajectories in our chat template. We introduce agentic data as soon as context extension begins rather than reserving it for post-training (5). Post-training. Post-training sharpens the model on selected domains, especially long-horizon agentic tasks. This is where our recipes differ most across model sizes, as we adjust the recipe to fit the capability of each model. For our 375B flagship model, we choose the final mid-training checkpoint as the starting point. Based on it, separate RL expert is trained for each of five domains: search, knowledge work, tool use, scientific reasoning, and instruction following with abstention. In each, the model acts in an environment such as sandbox, search engine, or simulated user, verifier scores the outcome, and the model is updated to favor successful behavior (6.3). The experts are then merged into single model by weight merging, which takes few minutes and retains most of each experts gains (6.4). Evaluating the merged model reveals the remaining gaps, such as unfamiliar agent harness formats, and final round of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on demonstrations targets them. Evaluation. Evaluation runs throughout the lifecycle, both to track progress and to catch regressions, and its findings feed back into later data and training stages (Sections 3.4 and 7). Finally, the model is optimized for efficient inference (10) and checked for safety (11). 6 Pre-training Mid-training Math RL Code RL Other RL experts SFT MOPD event 0 10 20 40 50 60 70 80 100 110 120 130 140 160 days 375B-A23B 120 days 36B-A4B 115.1 days 32B 159.5 days 7B 91 days 3.7B 106 days 0.9B 58 days new data mix ckpt avg. merge phase 1: 44.7 phase 2: 43.4 18.2 reasoning 4.7 search 2.8 tool use 2.7 knowledge work 2.3 IF & abstention 1.0 mid-training 29.6 Pre + mid only; 8k 32k 128k 512k pre-training 85.5 Pre + mid only; 8k 32k 128k 512k pre-training 59.7 pre-training 116.1 ckpt avg. sections.title:
2 Architecture
The K2-Horizon series retains the established Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) architecture, including
GQA (Ainslie et al., 2023), rotary positional embedding (RoPE; Su et al. 2021), SwiGLU (Shazeer, 2020),
and sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) (Shazeer et al., 2017; Lepikhin et al., 2021; Fedus et al., 2022).
sections.content: Table 1 summarizes the configurations. Training budgets and optimization are covered in 3.1. The 0.9B model targets memory-constrained mobile deployment. It uses 64,256-token vocabulary, compared with 250,624 tokens for the larger models. For the 3.7B, 7B, and 32B dense models, we adopt the depth, hidden width, and attention-head configurations of Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Qwen3-32B, respectively, as established architectural baselines (Yang et al., 2025). The two MoE models (36B-A4B and 375B-A23B) use fine-grained sparse mixture-of-experts layers with routed and shared experts, following DeepSeekMoE (Dai et al., 2024). Both keep dense feed-forward networks in the first three layers. Beyond the commonly used modules, we also introduce three components to improve capability and training stability: grouped RMSNorm, mixture-of-value attention (MoVA), and softplus attention gate.

sections.title:
2.1 Grouped RMSNorm
To facilitate the description of the new techniques, we use X = {x1, x2, . . . , xn} ∈ Rn×d and Y =
{y1, y2, . . . , yn} ∈ Rn×d to denote the input and output sequences with length n, and assume the
representations of the input and output sequences have the same dimension d.
sections.content: Root Mean Square Layer Normalization. The root mean square layer normalization mechanism (RMSNorm) (Zhang and Sennrich, 2019) simplifies the original layer normalization (LayerNorm) (Ba et al., 2016) by dropping the re-centering (mean subtraction) and bias terms, and instead individually re-scaling each input vector xt, {1, . . . , n} with its root mean square statistic: (cid:118) (cid:117) (cid:117) (cid:116) 1 xt,j vt vt = yt,j = (cid:88) i=1 x2 t,i + ϵ , {1, . . . , d} (1) (2) where we omit the commonly used scaling parameter for simplicity. RMSNorm achieves performance comparable to LayerNorm at lower computational cost, and has been adopted as the default normalization mechanism in range of frontier large language models (Touvron et al., 2023; Meta AI, 2024; Qwen Team et al., 2025; DeepSeek-AI et al., 2024). Theoretically, each output element yt,j lies in the range ( d). d, While typical element has magnitude around 1, this bound grows with model width (e.g., 90 for = 8192). As result, individual outputs of RMSNorm can become disproportionately large in wide models, which may lead to training instability in extreme cases. Grouped RMSNorm. We propose Grouped RMSNorm and apply it to the 3.7B, 7B, 32B, and 36B-A4B models. Formally, Grouped RMSNorm first partitions the feature dimensions of each xt into groups, with dg = d/k elements per group. The root mean square (RMS) statistic (3) is then computed independently within each group: vt,g = (cid:118) (cid:117) (cid:117) (cid:116) 1 dg (cid:88) iGg x2 t,i + ϵ, = 1, . . . , k. (3) By controlling the group dimension dg through the number of groups k, particularly by increasing as the model dimension grows, Grouped RMSNorm provides an explicit upper bound on the magnitude of each normalized output element, restricting it to the range ((cid:112)dg, (cid:112)dg). Empirical results demonstrate that Grouped RMSNorm substantially improves training stability across wide range of model scales in the K2-Horizon series.

MoE models extend standard transformer architectures by replacing the feed-forward network (FFN) with experts and routing function that sparsely selects subset for each token (Shazeer et al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2022). Given token representation x, the router assigns probabilities over experts and activates only the top-k: MoE(x) = (cid:88) iK(x) pi(x) Ei(x), where K(x) {1, . . . , E} with K(x) = denotes the selected expert indices and pi(x) are the normalized routing weights. Since in practice, per-token floating-point operations (FLOPs) scale with k, enabling parameter count to grow quasi-independently of computation. In practice, each expert Ei is instantiated as two-layer MLP network with SwiGLU activation (Shazeer, 2020). Unlike conventional MoE layers, where each expert Ei typically consists of two-layer 10 MLP and thus introduces nonlinearity, an individual value projection in (5) is purely linear. To introduce nonlinearity into the resulting value vector V(xt) in (6), we therefore apply SiLU activation function to (cid:1), pi(xt)W (i) the output of each value projection. Without this activation, the mixture reduces to xt an input-dependent linear map whose only nonlinearity comes from the routing weights. (cid:0) (cid:80) MoVA opens second axis for scaling sparsity in an LLM, beyond MoE in the FFN module. Importantly, MoVA enjoys the following advantages: Compatibility with efficient attention. MoVA only modifies how each value vector is computed from its own token, leaving the attention computation itself unchanged. It is therefore directly compatible with FlashAttention, GQA, and sparse attention. No additional KV cache. Each vt is fully determined once token is processed, so only the mixed value vector is cached, with the same size as in standard GQA. K2-Horizon-MoVA-36B-A4B combines MoVA with MoE FFN layers and activates about 4.6B parameters per token. Empirically, its pre-training loss closely tracks that of our 32B dense model, which was trained on the same data with identical settings, with the dense model maintaining modest lead. Downstream evaluations reflect this: at 1.1M steps, MoVA trails the dense model by only 1.2 to 3.7 points on MMLU, GSM8K, HellaSwag, and HumanEval, despite activating roughly one-seventh as many parameters (see 3.4 and full evaluation logs at W&B1).

sections.title:
2.3 Softplus Activation in Attention Gate
In the K2-Horizon-MoVA-36B-A4B model, we use gated attention with a softplus gate activation. The
gated attention mechanism has been extensively studied and widely used in frontier models (Hua et al.,
2022; Ma et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2026, 2023). Notably, Ma et al. (2023) show that gating
substantially increases the expressiveness of attention: single-head gated attention is as expressive as
multi-head attention.
sections.content: Formally, the gated attention mechanism applies gating vector to the attention output: γ = ϕ(XWγ + bγ) (cid:19) (cid:18) (cid:18) QKT τ (X) = (cid:19) γ, (7) (8) where denotes element-wise product, and ϕ() is the activation function used to compute the attention gate. Two common choices for ϕ() are sigmoid and SiLU, and Qiu et al. (2025) empirically show that sigmoid slightly outperforms SiLU. However, sigmoid is bounded in (0, 1): at initialization it sits near sigmoid(0) = 0.5, halving the attention output, and even at its maximum it can only recover the ungated output, never amplify it. This limits the expressiveness of the gate, since the result of Ma et al. (2023) requires the gate to represent the ratio between multi-head and single-head attention outputs, which can exceed 1. We therefore adopt the softplus function as the gate activation: softplus(x; β) = 1 β log (1 + exp(β x)) , (9) where β is scaling coefficient. Like sigmoid, softplus is strictly positive, so the gate acts as pure element-wise scaling factor; unlike sigmoid, it is unbounded above, allowing the gate to both attenuate and amplify. Moreover, setting β = log 2 yields softplus(0; log 2) = 1, so that at initialization, when the gate 1https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb/llm360/K2-Horizon-36B, https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb/llm360/K2-H orizon-32B 11 pre-activations are close to zero, the gate is approximately the identity and gated attention behaves like standard attention.

3.1.1 Pre-Training Hyperparameter Selection
AdamW timescale. Following Wang and Aitchison (2025); Bergsma et al. (2025), we express the coupling
between learning rate, weight decay, and training duration through the nominal AdamW timescale:
sections.content: τepoch = ηλD = 1 ηλT , (10) where is the global batch size in tokens, is the training token budget, = D/B is the number of optimizer steps, η is the peak learning rate, and λ is the weight-decay coefficient. The timescale expresses how quickly weight decay discounts earlier parameter values, measured as fraction of the training budget. Holding it fixed as learning rate or training length changes keeps the nominal accumulated decay comparable. Because the timescale is defined using the peak learning rate, it provides only nominal measure; the accumulated decay also depends on the learning-rate schedule. We used small-scale experiments to inform timescale selection and the corresponding production weight-decay settings. sections.title:
3.1.3 Mid-Training and Long-Context Recipe
Mid-training has three jobs: to realize the learning-rate decay that pre-training postponed, to extend the
context window from 8k to 512k tokens, and to shift the data toward long documents, reasoning, and
agentic trajectories (§5). It reuses each model’s pre-training batch size, weight decay, and peak learning
rate, so no new sweep is needed (Table 3).
sections.content: Implicit decay via merging. Because pre-training ends at the peak learning rate (3.1.2), mid-training starts from an average of the last few pre-training checkpoints rather than from single one, which acts as an implicit decay (Tian et al., 2026). Stage 1 then re-warms the learning rate to the pre-training peak and decays it linearly to 10% of the peak. Stage 1 carries most of the mid-training budget, about 1.1T of roughly 1.9T tokens, so this is where the explicit decay happens. Extending the context. Context then grows in three steps, from 32k tokens in stage 1 to 128k in stage 2 and 512k in stages 3 and 4, and these longer-context stages use far fewer tokens than stage 1. As in K2-V2 (K2 Team, Institute of Foundation Models, 2025), the learning rate stays at the 10% floor through stages 24 to keep optimization stable as the context grows, and the RoPE base rises with the context 14 length, from 500,000 in pre-training to 1 million in stage 1 and 10 million from stage 2 onward, so that rotary positions stay distinguishable over longer distances (Xiong et al., 2023). The 0.9B model. The 0.9B differs because its pre-training already ended with cosine decay, so it skips checkpoint averaging. After brief context-extension phase of about 2,000 steps on separate data, it runs two stages at 40k and 128k tokens of context, each with short warmup and cosine decay to 1% of the stages peak. It stops at 128k to keep its memory footprint within the budget of the phones and other memory-constrained devices it targets. Its first stage uses 40k rather than 32k tokens because its smaller vocabulary turns the same text into more tokens, so data prepared for 32k context would otherwise be truncated.

sections.title:
3.2.1 Clusters, Storage, and Reliability
Compute environment. All models in the K2-Horizon family were trained on servers with the same
node configuration as the K2-V2 cluster (K2 Team, Institute of Foundation Models, 2025, Sec. 3.4.1). Each
node hosts eight NVIDIA H200 GPUs (141 GB HBM, 700 W TDP) and two Intel Xeon Platinum 8468
CPUs with approximately 1.6 TB of system memory. For inter-node communication, each node is equipped
with eight 400 Gb/s InfiniBand NDR host channel adapters, one per GPU, for an aggregate of 3.2 Tb/s
of injection bandwidth per node. All nodes are connected through a fully non-blocking fabric. Jobs are
scheduled with Slurm. The fleet is shared with other workloads, and training runs are submitted under
dedicated accounts and quality-of-service (QoS) levels that govern priority and preemption.
sections.content: Storage and checkpointing. Checkpoints are distributed and sharded: all ranks cooperatively save and reload model shards, while optimizer shards are written once per non-replicated shard by designated ranks. This enables parallel checkpoint I/O and resumption. We write checkpoint about every 250 training steps to make potential rollbacks convenient. To bound storage use, older checkpoints are rotated out over time, while subset is retained (milestone checkpoints, usually every 5000 steps) for evaluation. For durability beyond the cluster filesystem, scheduled upload job copies completed checkpoints to Amazon S3. Reliability tooling. Runs are managed through an in-house submitter that wraps Slurm and exposes three lifecycle operations. Submit launches run, terminate stops it cleanly, and recover relaunches it from the most recent valid checkpoint. At the scale of our runs, hardware faults and transient job failures are expected. We therefore treat automatic restarts as routine operation and distinguish them from interventions, meaning deliberate human changes to runs configuration, data, or code. 3.3.2 reports the spikes detected during the run and the rollbacks they led to. Loss monitor. Alongside the fault-driven restarts above, separate monitor watches the training loss itself. Every 30 minutes it reads the most recent 35 minutes of per-step loss and applies two tests. The restart test flags window of 10 consecutive steps in which every loss exceeds 0.97 and the largest exceeds 1.2; requiring the whole window to stay high ignores isolated noisy steps, while the second condition requires large excursion. flag triggers rollback, and the run is relaunched through the submitter from the last checkpoint on the 250-step grid at or before the first flagged step. The alert test is looser (windows of 5 steps, with thresholds 0.95 and 0.99) and only sends notification. Both sets of thresholds are absolute loss values, so they encode the loss range of the run and must be retuned if it shifts. The monitor reads 15 the training loss only, and it has no guard against resuming repeatedly from the same checkpoint. 3.3.2 counts restarts and rollbacks by how far the run was rewound, whichever mechanism triggered them. The design follows the monitor used for K2-V2 (K2 Team, Institute of Foundation Models, 2025).

sections.title:
3.2.2 Training Infrastructure and Parallelism
Framework. All models are trained with xLLM, our in-house training framework, which we open
source alongside this report. xLLM is designed to be an efficient, production-tested infrastructure that
combines large-scale performance with research flexibility. Architectures, data mixtures, training stages,
and objectives can be changed without rebuilding the surrounding stack. It covers the full model lifecycle:
training, evaluation, checkpoint conversion, bridges to serving systems, and runtime kernels. xLLM was
already the mid-training framework for K2-V2, though it was not named in that report (K2 Team, Institute
of Foundation Models, 2025). For K2-Horizon we extended it to pre-training, so a single codebase now
spans multiple training stages.
sections.content: Parallelism trade-offs. Each parallelism axis trades memory savings for communication cost. We summarize the axes we use, following K2 Team, Institute of Foundation Models (2025, Sec. 3.4.2). Data parallelism (DP) splits each global batch across workers, and each worker processes its own shard of the batch. In its plain form, every worker holds full model replica, and gradients are synchronized with an all-reduce after each step (Li et al., 2020). This scales throughput almost linearly but saves no memory. xLLM instead implements DP with PyTorch FSDP in full-shard mode, which is equivalent to ZeRO-3 (Rajbhandari et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2023). Parameters, gradients, and optimizer states are sharded across the DP group of each tensor-parallel rank. Parameters are all-gathered one layer at time for compute and resharded after the forward pass. Gradients are reduce-scattered in fp32, not all-reduced. Each GPU therefore holds roughly 1/(TP DP) share of the model and optimizer state. The price is an extra parameter all-gather in both the forward and backward passes, and FSDP overlaps it with computation. Tensor parallelism (TP) shards individual weight matrices by rows or columns, so each device computes slice of every layer (Shoeybi et al., 2019). This cuts per-device parameter and activation memory, but it needs collectives inside every layer, in both the forward and backward passes. Only high-bandwidth intra-node links (NVLink) can absorb that traffic, so we restrict TP to 8-GPU groups within node. Expert parallelism (EP), which K2-V2 did not need, distributes the experts of mixture-of-experts layer across devices. Tokens are routed to their assigned experts through all-to-all communication (Lepikhin et al., 2021; Fedus et al., 2022). In xLLM, EP and TP are tied: experts are sharded across the same 8-GPU group used for tensor parallelism. Both axes therefore share one intra-node communication domain, and the all-to-all traffic never crosses the InfiniBand fabric. Context parallelism (CP) partitions activations along the sequence dimension, and its benefit grows with context length: activation memory scales with sequence length while parameter memory does not. xLLM has no separate sequence-parallel (SP) axis (Korthikanti et al., 2023). Between layers, tensor parallelism already shards activations along the hidden dimension. Our CP uses the all-gather formulation (Grattafiori et al., 2024). Each CP rank holds contiguous chunk of the sequence. For attention, it all-gathers keys and values from the other ranks and keeps only the causal prefix its queries need. CP ranks share parameters, so FSDP switches to hybrid sharding: parameters are sharded across DP and replicated across CP. We use no CP during 8k pre-training. CP is added in mid-training as context grows, and it reaches CP=4 at 512k context for the 375B flagship. Pipeline parallelism (PP) assigns contiguous groups of layers to different devices. xLLM has no pipeline axis. Pipelining introduces idle bubbles unless the per-device batch is large enough to fill the pipeline. 16 K2-V2 showed that, at its operating point, the bubble overhead outweighed the memory benefit (K2 Team, Institute of Foundation Models, 2025, Sec. 3.4.2), and the same reasoning applies at ours. Chosen strategy. For the 375B-A23B, these heuristics yield two-axis layout. Tied TPEP=8 runs within each node, and fully sharded (ZeRO-3) data parallelism spans all remaining devices. We use no context parallelism during 8k-context pre-training and defer it to the mid-training configuration. Master weights are kept in fp32 and sharded by FSDP. Forward and backward compute runs in bf16, and gradient reduction is performed in fp32. To save activation memory, we use selective recomputation: the gated-FFN intermediate activations are recomputed in the backward pass, while the output logits are kept. Attention uses FlashAttention. Smaller models reuse the same framework at smaller allocations  (Table 4)  and different recomputation controls to satisfy memory requirements. CP

sections.content: (cid:17) Loss spikes persist throughout training Spikes occur throughout the run, not only early. Counting episodes on erased branches, as K2-V2 does, we find that 43% to 67% of the spike episodes in the six runs that held constant peak learning rate fall in the first 40% of the run, compared with the vast majority in K2-V2; only the 0.9B run, whose learning rate decays on cosine schedule, is front-loaded (91%; Table 5). likely reason is that these runs hold the peak learning rate for most of training, whereas the 0.9B runs decaying learning rate suppresses later spikes. Many of the flagships spike episodes occurred on training branches that were later discarded when the run resumed from an earlier checkpoint, so they never entered the shipped model: 69% of the phase-1 episodes and 35% of the phase-2 episodes. Most spikes are brief, and the gradient norm gives little warning: it carries information only in the last ten steps before spike. This subsection describes how the training runs went, focusing on the 375B flagship and covering the smaller models more briefly. 3.3.1 describes the phase transition, which divided the flagship pre-training run into two regimes with separate step counters. 3.3.2 analyzes the loss spikes detected across both regimes, the restarts and rollbacks used to resolve them, and their cost in discarded training  (Table 5)  . 3.3.3 covers the mid-training run. The loss monitor used on the flagship run is described in 3.2.1.

sections.title:
3.3.2 Pre-Training Dynamics & Stability
This subsection describes how the pre-training runs behaved, with a focus on the 375B flagship: how the
loss evolved across models, how we detect and count loss spikes, whether the gradient norm warns of them,
and how restarts and rollbacks were used to handle them.
sections.content: Loss across scales. The 3.7B, 7B, 32B, and 36B-A4B models trained on the same 22T-token corpus, in two data orders: the 3.7B and 36B saw the same batches at every step, as did the 7B and 32B. Their normalized losses follow nearly the same trajectory (Figure 4). Each models loss is divided by its median over the final 1% of steps and plotted against progress after warmup. The normalization aligns the endpoints by construction; it does not force the earlier part of the curves to agree. The agreement spans dense and sparse models and nearly an order of magnitude in parameters, and is consistent with Bergsma et al. (2026), who find that loss curves collapse when hyperparameters are scaled together with the training budget, as ours are (3.1.1). Loss spikes. Loss spikes sharp, transient jumps in the training loss that interrupt an otherwise smoothly decaying curve are recurrent instability of large language model pre-training (Molybog et al., 2023; Takase et al., 2025). They have been linked to aggressive learning-rate schedules and to lagging second-moment estimate in Adam-style optimizers (Shazeer and Stern, 2018; Wortsman et al., 2023). Unlike K2-V2, whose learning rate followed cosine decay from the start (K2 Team, Institute of Foundation Models, 2025), our pre-training runs held the peak learning rate for the whole run, except for the 0.9B, whose cosine schedule decays to 10% of the peak. This difference may matter for when spikes occur (see below). To quantify spikes across the complete pre-training history of every K2-Horizon run on common scale, we use the robust local z-score of K2 Team, Institute of Foundation Models (2025), which measures how abnormal the current loss is relative to its recent history. For loss values yt over training steps t, we compute rolling median mt over trailing window (t) spanning 1% of the full training duration; to estimate the local variability of curve whose level falls throughout training, we take, within 19 each window, the median of the absolute deviations from the rolling median: MADt = mediansW (t) (cid:12) (cid:12) ys ms (cid:12) (cid:12), zt = yt mt 1.4826 MADt . (12) We flag loss spike wherever zt > 5. One spike episode runs from the first step with zt > 5 until zt stays below 2 for three consecutive steps, and later excursion starts new episode. Intuitively, zt reports how many typical fluctuations given step lies above the local baseline, adapting to the local noise level as the loss falls. run is often resumed from checkpoint: from the latest one (a restart, rewinding at most the 250-step checkpoint interval) or from an earlier one (a rollback, rewinding further). run that is resumed repeatedly leaves two histories: the accepted trajectory, the chain of checkpoint-resumed segments that led to the final model, and the branches abandoned along the way, whose rows on superseded segments cover step ranges that were later replayed. We apply the definition to both histories (K2 Team, Institute of Foundation Models, 2025), treating the spikes on abandoned branches as candidate failure events. Spikes on both histories are scored against the robust statistics (mt, MADt) of the accepted trajectory alone, so an excursion has one consistent meaning across all runs. Table 5 lists, for each run, its length and its counts of spike episodes and rollbacks. Spikes across the fleet. Table 5 applies the same detector to every pre-training run. Four runs trained stably: the 0.9B, 3.7B, 32B, and 36B models were rolled back at most 1.2 times per 100,000 steps. The 7B (3.9) and the flagship (13.8 in phase 1, 4.6 in phase 2) were not. The flagships spikes are brief but heavy-tailed: half of its phase-1 episodes last four steps or fewer, yet the median phase-1 episode peaks at 17 and the largest at 950 (Figure 5). Spikes also persist late into training (Figure 7b). In K2-V2, the vast majority of spikes fall in the first 40% of training (K2 Team, Institute of Foundation Models, 2025), For our 32B model, the closest counterpart to K2-V2s dense architecture, only 52% fall in the first 40% when counted the same way (including episodes on erased branches). We hypothesize that the long constant-learning-rate phase is the reason. Gradient norm. The gradient norm gives little warning of loss spike. We modeled the per-step probability that spike begins as function of the gradient norm in the preceding steps, controlling for the time since the last spike, the number of recent spikes, and the time since the last restart. In both phases, the only window with clear signal is the last ten steps: each standard deviation of elevation in the log gradient norm over those steps multiplies the odds of spike by 1.9 in phase 1 and 1.8 in phase 2. Excursions 11 to 100 steps earlier add nothing measurable, and their confidence intervals span one in both phases. This rise is close enough to the onset that it may be part of the spike itself, so we do not read it as an independent warning. The reported norm is measured before clipping, which at threshold of 1.0 engaged on about 1.5% of executed steps in phase 1 and 0.5% in phase 2 (Figure 6). Findings and interventions. On the 375B flagship, large share of the instability never reached the final model, because it occurred on branches that were later discarded when training resumed from checkpoint; the share is larger in phase 1 than in phase 2. Counting spike episodes at every logged step, phase 1 has 83 episodes on the accepted trajectory and 184 on erased branches; phase 2 has 71 and 38, respectively. Erased branches thus account for 69% of phase-1 episodes and 35% of phase-2 episodes (Figure 7a; Table 5). Our standard response to spike was to resume from the latest checkpoint. In 40 cases we instead rolled back to an earlier checkpoint: 29 times in phase 1 and 11 times in phase 2. Of these 40 rollbacks, 35 followed spike episode, and the deepest rewound 4,217 steps (Figure 7a). 20 Figure 5: Spike shapes in the flagship. (a) single-step transient in phase 1, peaking at about 15 times the usual fluctuation above the baseline (loss 1.07 against 0.89); training continues unaffected. (b) wide excursion in phase 1 that begins at step 84,114 on branch later erased by rollback: the loss rises from about 0.9 to 5.4, stays above 2 for 151 steps and is still above baseline when the branch ends at step 84,547. The run then resumes from step 82,001, and the final trajectory over the same steps (blue) shows no excursion. (c, d) Distributions of episode duration and of peak z-score (Equation 12) on the accepted trajectory, for the two phases; triangles mark the examples in (a) and (b), and the wide excursion lies on an erased branch and is not counted. Rollbacks in practice. The loss monitor (3.2.1) answers spike by restarting from checkpoint. Engineers add manual rollbacks when needed. The following example shows how automatic restarts and manual rollbacks interact. Near step 199,555 the loss jumped from about 0.9 to about 18, and the run was resumed from the checkpoint at step 199,500. The replay spiked again at nearly the same place: across ten resumes, five of the six attempts that reached step 199,538 spiked there, with onsets between steps 199,538 and 199,542. Only deeper rollback, to step 196,000, broke the pattern; its replay passed this point without spike, as did four later resumes at step 199,500. The trouble then moved forward instead of disappearing. Spikes recurred near steps 199,860 and 199,900 and again near 200,520, where the run was resumed from the checkpoint at step 200,500 more than forty times, and training moved past this stretch only after rollback to step 200,000. This stretch shows that the monitor can resume repeatedly from the same checkpoint when spike replays at the same step (Figure 8). We leave this unguarded on purpose: repeated failures at one step flag the checkpoint for an engineer, who then decides how far to roll back.

sections.title:
3.3.3 The Mid-Training Run
Mid-training, which ran at a lower learning rate, was more stable than pre-training. It ran in four stages,
each continuing from the end of the previous one: stage 1 at 32k context, stage 2 at 128k, and stages 3 and
4 at 512k. The learning-rate schedule and token budgets are given in §3.1.3, and the parallel layout, which

sections.title:
3.4 Base Model Evaluation
We evaluate K2-Horizon at every model size after each stage of mid-training. Our curriculum introduces
agentic, instruction-following, and conversational data early (§5), so intermediate checkpoints are not
directly comparable to external models: they have an advantage over base models and a disadvantage
against fully post-trained ones. We therefore report these results as reference points for how capabilities
evolve across pre-training and mid-training.

To understand how K2-Horizon acquires and refines its capabilities, we track its performance trajectory continuously across both the pre-training and mid-training phases. We open-source the W&B3 runs for all training stages and model sizes, which include regular benchmark evaluations conducted throughout each phase to offer high resolution performance data. Figure 10 shows the evolution of performance on few selected benchmarks for the 375B-A23B variant, across phase 2 of pre-training and mid-training stages 1-4. These benchmarks were not measured during Phase 1 pre-training. Interestingly, BBH and MBPP exhibit sharp but transient performance drops during Mid 4. Both recover at the following checkpoint, and neither drop coincides with noticeable change in training loss. This behavior is even more pronounced during mid-training stage 1 of the 3.7B model. sections.title:
4 Pre-Training Data
Our 3.7B, 7B, and 32B dense models and the 36B-A4B model were pre-trained on 22T tokens, and the
375B MoE model on about 15T tokens in two phases (Table 2). The natural data portion builds on
TxT360, the pre-training corpus of K2-V2 (K2 Team, Institute of Foundation Models, 2025), which we
extend with two more web crawls, ClueWeb and HPLT (§4.1), with public datasets for web text, code, and
math (§4.6), and with multilingual corpora covering 17 languages (§4.7). The bigger change from K2-V2 is
synthetic data: about 10T of the tokens we train on are synthetic, and nearly 17% of the corpus consists of
problem-solving trajectories with explicit reasoning (Sections 4.2, 4.3, and 4.4).
sections.content: 3https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb/llm360/projects 26 Figure 10: Evaluation performance of the 375B-A23B model during Phase 2 pre-training and four mid-training stages. Shaded regions indicate the training stages. Phase 2 and mid-training results use distinct markers because their evaluation protocols differ, so discontinuities between the two curves should not be interpreted as direct performance gains. Maximizing distribution support. Our goal for synthetic data is to expand the models support beyond natural data. We synthesize data both to re-balance the training distribution toward target domains and to add content that is scarce or absent in natural data, such as explicit reasoning. This includes reasoning traces for 250M math problems (4.2) and 259M synthesized programming tasks (4.3), reasoning on instructions with verifiable constraints (4.4), and texts that exhibit behaviors such as planning, weighing alternatives, or counterfactual reasoning (4.5). Our hypothesis is that base model with broader support is better prepared for post-training. This is motivated by our K2-V2 (K2 Team, Institute of Foundation Models, 2025) work where we introduced reasoning in mid-training and by prior work on the relation between base-model support and RL (Yue et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Gandhi et al., 2025). Diversity first. Broad support requires diverse data. At trillions of tokens, synthetic data easily collapses into few repetitive patterns, making diversity the main constraint in our data design. We address this with two techniques. First, we introduce diversity knobs: independent attributes of prompt that are sampled and combined, so that the number of distinct prompts grows combinatorially with the number of Figure 11: Evaluation performance and training loss of the 3.7B model across pre-training and four mid-training stages. The left panel reports MMLU-Pro, GSM8K, and MBPP at their available checkpoints; distinct markers denote the different evaluation protocols used during pre-training and mid-training. The right panel shows train loss, sampled at the same checkpoints. Figure 12: document is dataset of tokens: each token is label for the context before it. An error such as 2 + 2 = 5 is one mislabeled token, and the tokens around it remain correct labels. This is why we do not discard synthetic trajectories that contain mistakes. knobs. This combinatorial explosion yields tens of billions of distinct prompts (e.g., 6.6 1010 conceptknob combinations for programming tasks; 4.3). Second, we ground synthesis in documents retrieved by Search3604, our search index over 994M documents from our web corpus (4.5). To verify that this works, we measure diversity by compression with WZIP, our own compressor: less diverse corpus compresses better, and our final pipelines closely track the compression trend of natural web and code data (Figure 14). No verification in synthetic pre-training data. Most of our synthetic data is not verified: math solutions are not checked against reference answers, and generated code is not executed. We view each document as dataset of tokens, in which every token is label for the context before it (Figure 12). trajectory that ends with wrong answer still contains thousands of tokens of valid steps, notation, and techniques, and its few mislabeled tokens are ordinary label noise. Strict verification-based filtering would discard all of these tokens and reduce data diversity. We do filter defects that corrupt many tokens at once, such as truncated generations, leaked special tokens, and degenerate loops. Mixing for the target scale. Which mix is best depends on scale. Math and SFT-style data help small models quickly but saturate, while web text pays off as model capacity grows. We therefore chose the mix by fitting scaling laws on small models and predicting benchmark scores at production scale (4.9). The prediction reversed our decision: the mix that was best in 1.5B runs is predicted to be the worst of three at 32B  (Table 17)  . 4https://github.com/ifm-ai/search 28 (cid:17) Diversity beats mixing The largest gains came from new and diverse data, mostly synthetic pipelines with strict diversity control. Tuning the mix mattered less: at 32B, the predicted gap between our best and worst candidate mix is about two points on the benchmark average  (Table 17)  .

sections.title:
4.1 Web data
Our web-data collection builds on the source mixture and curation methodology used for K2-V2 (K2
Team, Institute of Foundation Models, 2025), combining large-scale web crawls with curated domain-
specific sources. For K2-Horizon, we extend this collection with ClueWeb (Overwijk et al., 2022) and
HPLT (Burchell et al., 2025).
sections.content: Data sources. The collection comprises the following sources, listed in descending order of cross-source deduplication priority: MegaMath, Wikipedia, HackerNews, StackExchange, PG-19, Ubuntu IRC, FreeLaw, Europarl, Europarl-Aligned, USPTO, arXiv, PhilPapers, S2ORC abstracts, S2ORC full text, PubMed abstracts, PubMed Central, Common Crawl, ClueWeb, and HPLT. Processing and deduplication. For sources shared with K2-V2, we follow the corresponding sourcespecific preprocessing and filtering procedures described in that report. The newly added ClueWeb (Overwijk et al., 2022) contributes an additional large-scale web crawl, while HPLT (Burchell et al., 2025) provides web text originating from Common Crawl and the Internet Archive. Both additions undergo the same processing and filtering pipeline used for Common Crawl in K2-V2, including language identification, URL filtering, line-level cleaning, document-level quality filtering, and removal of personally identifiable information. We apply global deduplication across the combined collection, retaining documents from higher-priority sources when duplicates are identified across sources.

sections.title:
4.1.1 Web Data Annotation, Curation, and Shuffling
Annotation. We annotated 6.754 trillion tokens across 7.751 billion web documents, excluding the txt360-qa
subset of TxT360 (Tang et al., 2024), whose QA-annotated passages duplicate web text already in the corpus.
Following the ensemble bucketing approach of Nemotron-CC (Su et al., 2024), we combined FineWeb-Edu,
fastText ELI5, and fastText PreSelect scores. Each score was mapped to one of 20 ordered buckets using
fixed thresholds; the maximum bucket index determined the document’s quality tier (Table 10). This
retains documents rated highly by any classifier. We additionally assigned topic and format labels with
WebOrganizer’s TopicClassifier and FormatClassifier, which each distinguish 24 categories (Wettig et al.,
2025).
sections.content: Filtering and curation. We converted heterogeneous inputs, primarily JSONL, to typed Parquet for compact columnar storage and selective reads. The resulting annotations supported construction of the web-high and web-high-medium training subsets. Lazy queries in Polars enabled filtering by quality, topic, format, and document length, and aggregation of counts and scores to compare candidate data mixtures at scale. We used party for document inspection. We release party and other tools we developed for working with pre-training data.

(cid:17) Inspecting the data is essential We found that directly inspecting documents was one of the most valuable practices in curating our pre-training corpus. To make this easy, we developed party, command-line tool that randomly samples and displays documents from corpus files or directories across multiple formats, including JSON, JSONL, Parquet, and tokenized datasets. This simple workflow helped us uncover many issues in our data pipelines. Decompressing the web. web document is compressed record: it states its content but leaves implicit the many facts careful reader could derive from it, such as which words recur, which entities it concerns, or how often letter occurs. We make part of this latent content explicit by appending to each web-high document few questions about the document itself, with answers computed programmatically rather than generated by model. The augmentation adds no information that is not already in the document; it spells out the computation needed to extract it, so every answer is exact by construction and 30 the augmentation costs no GPU time. Each document was analyzed with spaCy (en_core_web_sm) for tokenization, part-of-speech tags, sentence boundaries, and named entities, where word is lowercased alphabetic token. From this analysis we instantiated 11 question templates in four families: Frequency: words that appear exactly three times, the longest word that appears more than twice, and the number of occurrences of random letter. Contextual filtering: the most frequent verbs excluding auxiliaries, words longer than six characters, and capitalized words that do not start sentence. Threshold and ranking: words that appear between five and ten times, and the three least common words that appear more than once. Semantic grouping: the most frequent action verbs and state verbs (separated by fixed list of state verbs), and the most frequent people, places, and organizations. For each document we sampled between one and five of the applicable questions uniformly, shuffled their order, and appended them after separator and fixed instruction to answer using only the text above. Answers are short sentences and include counts where the question asks for ranking. The pipeline was applied to all web-high documents longer than 300 words. <document text> --- Read the document above. Using only that text, compute word frequencies [...] Then answer the following questions precisely and concisely. Question: How many times does the letter 'g' occur in the above text? Answer: The letter 'g' occurs 28 times in the text. Question: Which words appear exactly 3 times in this document? Answer: The words that appear exactly 3 times are: not, it, they, product, can, is, with, and as. This data corresponds to TxT360-v2 in our release.

sections.title:
4.2 Math reasoning
Our math reasoning data starts from about 250 million unique problems (after exact deduplication) from a
variety of sources. These sources are drawn from permissively licensed mathematical datasets studied in
the OpenThoughts project (Guha et al., 2025)5. To reduce the risk of contamination, we use only training
splits where applicable. The resulting collection spans a broad range of problem types and difficulty levels,
including templated arithmetic and numerical tasks (e.g., determining whether a large number is prime),
verification of mathematical statements, and other mathematical reasoning problems. We previously used
this problem set to create mid-training data for K2-V2 (K2 Team, Institute of Foundation Models, 2025).
sections.content: Solutions with reasoning. We generate solutions for each of the problems with Qwen3-32B with thinking (Yang et al., 2025) and GPT-OSS-120B with high reasoning effort (Agarwal et al., 2025). Resulting pretraining documents are simple concatenation of problem statement, reasoning trace, and answer after removing chat template special tokens. We filter out samples that did not finish within 15.5k-token budget or contained unexpected special tokens (e.g., commentary or extra analysis channels for GPT-OSS). Resulting data consisted of 800B tokens for problems with Qwen3 generations and 424B for problems with GPT-OSS generations. 5https://www.open-thoughts.ai/blog/thinkagain 31 Socratic teacherstudent dialogues. Solution traces show single, uninterrupted line of reasoning. To also show how solver responds to feedback (spotting an error, revising an attempt, confirming result), we simulate tutoring dialogues between two LLM agents (Figure 13). Unlike the dialogue re-writes below, which recast an existing reasoning trace, these dialogues are generated interactively, and the student never sees the answer. We start from the hardest problems in our collection: those whose GPT-OSS-120B solution exceeded 8,192 tokens and that have reference answer, 8.1M problems in total. More than half of them (4.5M) ask whether large number is prime or composite (see the Is it prime? takeaway below), so we remove every problem that mentions either word, leaving 3.6M problems. All configurations draw from the same pool of 3.6M problems. Student tokens (reasoning and answers) are exact; total tokens add the teachers messages, estimated from their character count at the students characters-per-token ratio. Both agents are GPT-OSS-120B. The student receives only the problem and the system prompt You are an expert mathematician. The teacher receives the problem and its reference answer, which is usually short final answer rather than worked solution, and is instructed never to reveal it. The student opens with solution attempt. On each turn the teacher evaluates the latest attempt: if it is correct, the teacher explains why and ends the dialogue with an <END_CONVERSATION> token; otherwise it asks probing questions that break the problem into smaller steps or point at the faulty step, without correcting it directly. Each agent sees only the others messages, not its reasoning. We use two teacher prompts. The first is plain Socratic tutor. The second assigns the teacher random persona, covering profession, skills, hobbies, and location; the persona shapes the teachers voice and choice of move (a targeted question, micro-hint, an analogy, check), and the teacher makes one move per turn and accepts any valid method, not only the one in the reference. As second diversity knob, we vary the reasoning effort of both agents: low or medium for the student, and low, medium, or high for the teacher. We keep only dialogues that the teacher closed within 100 turns without errors. Each one becomes pre-training document with the student as the assistant: the students reasoning is kept, the teachers reasoning is dropped, and the teachers messages become user turns. The result is 8.1M dialogues with about 38B tokens, 27B of them from the student  (Table 11)  . Hard, prime-free problems are posed to student agent that sees only the problem. teacher agent that also sees the reference answer checks each attempt and either probes the students reasoning or, once the attempt is correct, ends the dialogue. The teacher prompt (plain Socratic or sampled persona) and both agents reasoning effort serve as diversity knobs. Completed dialogues are rendered as pre-training documents from the students perspective. Reasoning re-writes. LLM reasoning traces often contain detailed analysis, derivations, and references to relevant mathematical results. However, the style of LLM reasoning lacks diversity and can often appear unnatural. To convert knowledge and mathematical techniques from the reasoning traces into more natural text, we developed two re-writing pipelines that we applied to problems with Qwen3 reasoning and answers: Study guide re-write where we instruct GPT-OSS to Transform the following problem-solving trace into educational content that teaches the concepts and methods used. resulting in 566B tokens. Dialogue re-write inspired by MIND (Akter et al., 2025). We adopt five styles: debate, interview, problem_solving, teacher_student, and two_students. For each, we create our own prompt and use GPT-OSS to re-write Qwen3 reasoning and answers into the corresponding dialogue style resulting in 1.5T tokens. We release the full Math Reasoning data collection. (cid:17) Is it prime? When we examined the problems with the longest reasoning, we expected to find the hardest ones, but realized that most of them asked to check whether large number is prime or to find its prime factors. Such questions make up only 4% of our problems, yet account for 59% of Qwen3 and 70% of GPT-OSS generations that exceeded the token budget. More broadly, over 80% of the collected problems are procedurally generated, and we think that the diversity and quality of the problems can be substantially improved. However, we found that training on reasoning and solutions for these tasks is already quite effective, judging by the strong performance of our pre-trained model on math benchmarks.

sections.title:
4.3 Code reasoning
Unlike math, we did not have a large collection of programming problems to start from, so we had to
synthesize the tasks ourselves. The key challenge is diversity: simply asking an LLM to write a programming
problem over and over tends to produce similar ones. To address this, we seed every task with a random
combination of a programming concept, a snippet of real-world code, and a set of diversity knobs.
sections.content: Task synthesis. As programming concepts, we choose 1,304 reference implementations of algorithms and data structures in 66 categories (e.g., graphs, dynamic programming, string processing) from the TheAlgorithms/Python6 and keon/algorithms7 repositories. We pair each concept with random snippet of 2030 lines of Python code from RefineCode (Huang et al., 2025), which serves as inspiration for the setting and style of the task. Diversity knobs then control how precisely the task is specified (from vague user request to detailed competitive programming statement), its difficulty, framing (algorithmic, practical, academic, debugging, or optimization), constraint style, application domain (one of 90), and twelve binary switches such as input/output examples, starter code, multi-part structure, type hints, or test-driven development. The knobs alone give 50.3M distinct configurations, or 6.6 1010 conceptknob combinations, before accounting for the code snippets. We made five passes over the 57M Python files in RefineCode, synthesizing one task per file with GPT-OSS-120B with high reasoning effort: three passes use restricted set of knobs where every task is phrased as vague user request, and two passes use all knobs. After filtering out generations that were truncated or exceeded 7.5k tokens, we obtained 259M tasks. Even tasks sharing the same concept rarely overlap, with only 1% of 5-grams in common on average. Solutions with reasoning. We generate solutions with GPT-OSS-120B with high reasoning effort and 32k token budget. Similarly to math, pre-training documents are concatenation of the task, reasoning trace, and final answer. Code solutions tend to be long (median 8.6k tokens, and 11% exhaust the budget), so we split them by length: solutions within 15.5k tokens resulted in 100.7M documents (761B tokens), while longer ones (up to 31k tokens) resulted in 23.7M documents (543B tokens) that we reserved for mid-training. In both cases, we filter out solutions with stray channel markers. Tasks synthesized with all knobs tend to be more detailed and require longer solutions (median 10.5k vs. 7.7k tokens), so we release them as separate hard subsets. In addition, we release version without reasoning (task and final answer only; 210M documents, 790B tokens), an earlier version of the reasoning data (82M documents), and the task synthesis traces from one of the all-knobs passes (49M documents, 286B tokens). Finally, we reproduced the CodeI/O pipeline (Li et al., 2025c), which turns code into reasoning about predicting functions inputs and outputs, resulting in 23B tokens. We released the full Code Reasoning data collection. (cid:17) Good luck! When writing programming task, GPT-OSS can hardly resist wishing the solver well: 73% of synthesized tasks end with Good luck! (often with rocket emoji). We strip the sign-off when processing the tasks.

sections.title: 4.4 SFT reasoning
sections.content: 6https://github.com/TheAlgorithms/Python 7https://github.com/keon/algorithms

sections.title:
4.4.1 Instruction-following (IF) reasoning
Real instructions often come with hard requirements on the form of the answer, such as a word limit, a
keyword that must appear, or a fixed number of sections. Such requirements can be verified, which makes
them a source of reasoning data whose answers are verified without a judge. We synthesized prompts with
such constraints and used the responses, including the reasoning, in pre-training.
sections.content: Prompts. Each prompt pairs writing task (e.g., an essay, tutorial, professional email, or report on one of 15 topics) with one to five constraints drawn from 37 constraint types in 15 categories, following the taxonomy of verifiable instructions introduced by IFEval (Zhou et al., 2023a). The types cover keyword frequencies and exclusions, letter counts, the number of paragraphs, sentences, words, bullet points, and highlighted sections, the first and last word of the response or of paragraph, postscripts and placeholders, copying and repeating spans, the response language, and capitalization. Parameters such as keywords, counts, and positions are sampled for each prompt, and 13 incompatible pairs of types (e.g., two different requirements on the first word) are never combined. The number of constraints is skewed toward fewer constraints, from 41.5% of prompts with one to 1.9% with five. The writing tasks are our own templates, and no prompts are taken from evaluation sets. Responses and verification. We generated responses with GPT-OSS-120B (Agarwal et al., 2025) at low, medium, and high reasoning effort. Every constraint type has code-based verifier built on regular expressions and string operations, and we kept response only if it satisfied all constraints. We then removed exact duplicates of the user prompt. Pre-training documents concatenate the prompt, the reasoning trace, and the response, and we removed GPT-OSS-specific artifacts as for our other GPT-OSS data. The result is 8.6M documents with 44B tokens. The reasoning dominates: its median length is 3.6k tokens, compared with 465 tokens for the response. Deduplication also reshaped the mix: single-constraint prompts have few distinct instantiations, so their share fell from about half of the verified responses to 22%. This data is released as the instruction-following subset of SFT-Reasoning. (cid:17) Counting is the hard part Writing to specification is easy but checking it is not. Constraints that make the model count its own output dominate the reasoning: requirement such as the letter should appear 32 times occurs in 10% of prompts but in 35% of the longest tenth of reasoning traces, and all lowercase words should appear at most times raises the median reasoning length from 3.6k to 9.6k tokens. Including keyword or avoiding word takes 23k.

sections.title:
4.4.2 SFT data as pre-training text
TxT360-3efforts, the SFT data we released with K2-V2 (K2 Team, Institute of Foundation Models, 2025),
contains conversations in math, code, chat, STEM, instruction following, tool use and safety, with answers
mostly generated by GPT-OSS-120B (Agarwal et al., 2025) at low, medium and high reasoning effort. It is
a 9.5M-conversation mix sampled from a larger pool in which most questions are answered at all three
effort levels. We reuse this pool in pre-training by rendering each conversation, including the reasoning, as
plain text, so the same problem appears with reasoning of different lengths.
sections.content: Format diversity. Rendering tens of millions of conversations with single template would make the template one of the most repeated patterns in the data. We therefore draw format for every conversation. In 43% of conversations (68% of those with tools), the turns are marked with role labels drawn from 21 35 sets (e.g., User:/Assistant:, Human:/AI:, Markdown headers, bracketed or bold labels, and one-letter prefixes), combined with one of 7 turn separators and 7 wrappers around the conversation. The remaining conversations use one of eight other layouts: turns separated only by delimiter, document with sections (background, query, analysis, response), questionanswer pairs, instruction and response blocks, named personas, an interview transcript, screenplay, and compact format with one line per turn. Conversations with tools use only the four layouts that render tool definitions, calls and results, and show the list of tools in one of four styles. In every layout the reasoning precedes the response, in some under its own heading. The result is 32.2M documents with 79.5B tokens, released as the 3efforts-pretrain subset of SFTReasoning.

sections.title:
4.5 Pre-training Behaviors
The question augmentation of web-high makes explicit what a single document leaves implicit. Knowledge
about a topic, however, is spread across many documents, and web text rarely shows the behaviors we
want a model to acquire, such as explaining a concept to a novice, planning under constraints, weighing
alternatives, or reasoning from evidence to a conclusion. We decompress this knowledge across documents:
for each question, we retrieve the relevant documents from our pre-training corpus and ask a model to
write a text that exhibits a chosen behavior, grounded in what was retrieved. This data corresponds to
Pretrain-Behaviors in our release.
sections.content: Search index. We built Search3608, dense retrieval service over the corpus itself. It indexes web-high together with the High-Quality and Medium-High-Quality partitions of Nemotron-CC-v2.1 (NVIDIA, 2025a): 994M documents split into 4.0B passages of 128 tokens, where final passage shorter than 64 tokens is merged into the one before it. Passages are embedded with Contriever-MSMARCO (768 dimensions) (Izacard et al., 2021) and indexed with FAISS as an IVFPQ index with 4,096 centroids and 16 sub-quantizers of 8 bits, trained on 10M sampled embeddings and searched with 256 probes. The index stores no text. Arrays map each passage to its document and to byte offset in the original JSONL shards, so passage or full document is read with single seek. FastAPI service returns either passages or full documents, ranked by the number of retrieved passages they contain, with optional re-ranking by jina-reranker-v3. Behind round-robin load balancer with health checks, one 8-GPU node answered 1,000 queries in 53 at 64128 concurrent requests without re-ranking, or about 19 queries per second. Questions. We started from Quora questions and Natural Questions and asked an LLM to write five deeper follow-up questions for each, which gave about 6M questions. For each question we retrieved the top eight documents in full. Behaviors. Each prompt template specifies behavior and receives the question and the retrieved documents, which the generated text must draw on. The templates fall into four families  (Table 12)  . The general family has 58 genres, from research abstracts and legal memoranda to lesson plans, documentary scripts, and steelmanned critiques. The reasoning family has 47 modes of reasoning, such as counterfactual, first-principles, and game-theoretic reasoning. The planning family covers plans with risks and mitigations, timelines and dependencies, and fixed resource budgets, and the data science family covers machine learning system design, experimentation, and data analysis. We generated the texts with GPT-OSS-120B (Agarwal et al., 2025) at high reasoning effort and kept only the final text, without the reasoning. In document-grounded variant, each prompt also received three attributes sampled Diversity knobs. from 22, including mood, education level, writing style, perspective, narrative structure, audience, and 8https://github.com/ifm-ai/search360 factuality level, each with 3 to 21 values. The attributes are appended as constraints that the text must satisfy without naming them, so the same document yields, for example, speculative text for children or formal, first-person text for experts. In the main run, diversity comes from crossing the templates with the questions and their retrieved documents.

sections.content: 207M 630B 502M 1,324B 898B 290M 335B 123M 1.1B 3.18T Table 12: Search-grounded behavior data by template family. Measuring diversity. When synthesizing data at trillion-token scale, it is easy to miss repetitive patterns that the model may then learn to reproduce. To quantify diversity, we developed custom lossless compressor, WZIP. Its key distinction from Zlib/GZIP and Zstandard is the explicit coupling of matchlength-dependent sliding windows, dedicated hash indexes, and length-conditioned distance coding. Short matches use compact local histories and specialized distance models, while larger histories use longer, more selective hash seeds to identify distant repetitions. This design controls short-match coding costs and limits unnecessary candidate scanning while retaining access to long-range repetitions. The decoded match length selects the distance model without an additional per-match selector. Together with bounded searches and Huffman coding, this organization targets high compression throughput on large datasets. Under consistent evaluation settings, we use the compression ratio (input bytes per compressed byte) as quantitative proxy for textual redundancy to assess how our search and generation controls affect corpus diversity, complementing assessments of semantic coverage and data quality. In Figure 14, we present WZIP compression ratios for the reasoning pre-training behaviors, comparing them to an earlier version of this pipeline without search and diversity knobs, and to natural code and web data. Code and web data have different baseline compression ratios, but for both the ratio grows slowly with the number of documents due to natural data diversity. Our final pipeline nearly matches the compression ratio trend of natural data, while our earlier version lacks sufficient diversity. Compression ratio was among the key metrics guiding our synthetic data generation development.

sections.title:
4.6 Public sources
Alongside the corpora we build and release, our pre-training mixture includes public datasets for web text,
code, mathematics, and instruction-style data (Table 13). Public multilingual corpora are described in §4.7.
sections.content: Web. We use Nemotron-CC-v2 (Su et al., 2024; NVIDIA, 2025b) and Nemotron-CC-v2.1 (NVIDIA, 2025a), discarding every partition below medium-high quality. About three quarters of the retained tokens are synthetic: rephrasings, translations into English, and question-answer pairs that the dataset authors generated from web documents. Code. As in K2-V2 (K2 Team, Institute of Foundation Models, 2025), our base source-code corpus is RefineCode (Huang et al., 2025). We add Stack-Edu (Allal et al., 2025), Nemotron-CC-Code-v1, and the synthetic code data of Nemotron-Pretraining-Code v1 and v2 (NVIDIA, 2025b,a). Math. We use the 3plus partition of Nemotron-CC-Math-v1 (Mahabadi et al., 2025), in addition to the MegaMath data in our web collection (4.1). 37 Figure 14: WZIP compression ratio versus the number of documents compressed together (log scale); higher ratio means less diverse text. Dashed lines are natural code and web data. v0 is an earlier version of our pipeline without search and diversity knobs. Instruction-style data. We include question-answer data in plain pre-training format from NemotronPretraining-SFT-v1 and Nemotron-Pretraining-Specialized-v1. From Nemotron-Pretraining-SFT-v1, we remove every sample whose recorded generating models include 72B-parameter Qwen2.5 model due to license restriction, which removes 39.9% of its samples; Nemotron-Pretraining-Specialized-v1 is used in full. We also include Nemotron-Post-Training-Dataset-v1 (Nathawani et al., 2025) and the Llama-Nemotron post-training data (Bercovich et al., 2025), after removing samples generated by Llama models and nonEnglish samples. We delete the <think> and </think> tags from these samples and keep the reasoning text between them. We use these datasets under their original licenses and do not redistribute them.

sections.title:
4.7 Multilingual data
Multilingual text makes up roughly 7% of our pre-training mixture and covers 17 languages (Table 14).
Three languages have a dedicated corpus: Arabic, French, and Hindi. For the remaining languages, we use
public web data and translated question-answer data.
sections.content: Arabic, French, and Hindi. As in K2-V2 (K2 Team, Institute of Foundation Models, 2025), our Arabic data is the corpus assembled for the Jais family of models (Sengupta et al., 2023). It contains Arabic web text from Common Crawl, public corpora such as ArabicWeb, OSCAR, CC100, Wikipedia, books and news. French is web text from RedPajama (Weber et al., 2024). Hindi is compiled from public corpora, primarily Sangraha (Khan et al., 2024), HPLT (Burchell et al., 2025), Common Crawl, FineWeb2, C4, and CulturaX, together with smaller community datasets. The three corpora contain 902M, 645M, and 256M documents, respectively. Broader language coverage. sections.title:
4.8 Benchmark decontamination
Benchmark contamination makes evaluation scores look better than the actual model performance. In a
corpus of our size, benchmark items can come in through web pages that quote them, through synthetic
data built from benchmark problems, or through public datasets that include evaluation splits. We therefore
scan all our training data for overlap with the benchmarks and remove the documents that match. A
benchmark item that was paraphrased or translated will not be found.
sections.content: Approach. We use the AllenAI decon tool (Allen Institute for AI, 2025) with few changes. We added Python bindings and stage that removes contaminated documents. We also use 8-token n-grams for questions, instead of the default 5, so that match needs longer overlap. Each benchmark item is split into question, answer, and an optional passage. This way document that copies only the question scores lower than one that copies the whole item. To find matches, we build an inverted index of hashed n-grams from the benchmark items and look for matching 8-gram in each training document. When one is found, the match is extended token by token. The overlap is then scored so that rare n-grams count more than common ones, and short items have to match more closely than long ones. We remove documents that score 0.85 or higher. Benchmarks. We prepared evaluation data for the 208 benchmarks in our registry and scanned every data source against all of them. After looking at the results for each benchmark and each dataset, we removed contamination for the 18 benchmarks we report results on. These make up 27 entries in the registry. For ARC and GSM8K, we only count matches with the test split. Removal. Each match records the file and line of the training document. Removal therefore only rewrites the files that have matches, and every removed line is logged. We remove the whole document and not just the matched text. Contamination is rare in all of our data. The highest rate, 0.026% of documents, is in the SFT reasoning data; the next highest, 0.017%, is in the pre-training behaviors data. In 35 of the 37 datasets with any match, the rate is 0.01% or lower. Table 15 shows what we removed: 197,149 matches in 88,625 documents from 30 datasets. Only 23 of the 27 registry entries had any match. The table does not include the SFT reasoning data and the Arabic corpus, whose removal had not finished when we collected these numbers. They add another 12,616 matches in 8,462 documents. Most removed matches are near-exact copies, and 172k of them score 0.95 or higher. MMLU and MMLU-Pro account for 166k matches, which is 84.6% of the total. About two thirds of the removed documents come from four datasets: the data science behaviors, the public instruction-style data, and two web datasets.

sections.title:
4.9 Data mix
The corpora above can be mixed in many ways, and the mix that looks best in a small ablation need not
be the mix that is best at the scale we actually train. The two ends of our design space make this concrete.
SFT-style and mathematical data are dense and immediately useful, but they are a small share of the
available tokens and their benefit saturates quickly. Web text is broad and high-entropy, and we expect it
to pay off as model capacity grows. We therefore chose the pre-training mix by comparing candidate mixes
on their predicted benchmark scores at the target scale rather than on their measured scores at small scale.
sections.content: Candidate mixes. We compared three candidates built from the same sources  (Table 16)  : web-heavy mix, math-heavy mix, and an SFT-heavy mix. They share the code sources and the multilingual budget, and differ mainly in how they divide the remaining budget between web text on one side and mathematical
