sections.title:
4.10 Tokenizer
The model uses a standard 256K byte-level BPE tokenizer (64K for 0.9B model) trained from scratch on a
custom multilingual and code-focused corpus of approximately 25.2 GB. The training mixture contains
about 9.9 GB of English, 5.9 GB of Arabic, 4.2 GB of code and structured text, and additional data spanning
Hindi, French, Bengali, Chinese, German, Persian, Filipino, Indonesian, Italian, Japanese, Malayalam,
Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, Turkish, and Urdu. The comparatively large Arabic allocation, roughly 24%
of the on-disk corpus before including Persian and Urdu, was designed to provide substantially stronger
Arabic coverage than general-purpose multilingual tokenizers. Code data includes general source code,
JSON, Python, SQL, shell, HTML, and TeX. When tuning the tokenizer training mix, we measured fertility
on our own code, TeX files from prior work, and synthesized examples of downstream use cases. This led
us to up-weight JSON and Python data, where our first tokenizer was less efficient than other open-model
tokenizers.
sections.content: Text is NFC-normalized and processed with Qwen-style Unicode-aware pre-tokenizer followed by byte-level BPE, including segmentation of long numerical strings into groups of up to three digits. The complete byte alphabet provides open-vocabulary coverage without an unknown token. The tokenizer includes BOS/EOS tokens plus markers for fill-in-the-middle coding, repository and notebook metadata, and tables. The 256K BPE model (64K for 0.9B model) is followed by 256 special-token IDs, comprising 50 functional markers and 206 reserved slots. 9The 375B run started before all data pipelines were finalized.

sections.title:
5 Mid- and Post-Training data
Our mid- and post-training data targets long context and agentic ability. Unlike common practice, we do
not separate these stages explicitly: agentic data enters as soon as context extension begins (§3.1.3), mixed
with long-context pre-training data, agentic data in both pre-training and chat formats, and additional
instruction-following and reasoning data. We developed many task generation pipelines and collected public
post-training datasets (§5.18). Together, they provide 106M unique documents and trajectories with 1.17T
tokens, with 75% of the trajectories coming from our own pipelines. The data carries over the philosophy
of our pre-training data (§4): diversity first, grounding in real data, and no verification in many pipelines.
sections.content: Grounding in real sources. Beyond Search360 (4.5), we use the Keenable web search API10 to find relevant sources such as repositories, office files, and papers, with about 5M requests supporting task synthesis. We also curate specialized collections of code and papers, which we query with simple keyword search when creating tasks. Our main curated source is PRism, collection of GitHub pull requests (5.1). Besides fueling four pipelines for agentic coding data (Figure 17), PRism turned out to be rich source of office files: its repositories contain 1.3M PDF, Word, Excel, and PowerPoint files, which we use to synthesize knowledge-work and file manipulation tasks (5.9.2). Diversity and strong teachers. Diversity remains our primary focus, but strong teacher is also essential. In SFT (6.6), we used the then newly released Kimi K3 (Kimi Team, 2026b) and DeepSeekV4-Flash (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) for both task synthesis and trajectory generation, which improved the performance of our model. teacher is limited by its own abilities, but the training data we generate does not have to be. We developed generation techniques that produce trajectories beyond what the teacher can do in single rollout (5.16). Multi-turn PR chains replay the PRs of repository as consecutive requests in one coding session: the teacher handles one PR at time, while the training trajectory captures the entire session and reaches hundreds of thousands of tokens (5.16.3). privileged advisor uses the reference solution and hidden tests to find the solvers mistakes and inserts targeted cues into its reasoning, without revealing the solution. Rerunning the tasks the solver failed with an advisor raises the share of tasks with successful trajectory from 54% to 73% (5.16.4). These techniques require extra compute for each trajectory, so we reserve them for the hardest tasks. AI for Science. particular focus of our data is AI for Science (5.12): tasks and environments built from research papers, simulated research community, Kaggle competitions, scientific simulators, and proofs from machine learning theory. Quality without verification. As in pre-training, many of these pipelines forgo verifying the final answer (Figure 12). Instead, every trajectory must pass strict programmatic checks of format and behavior (5.17). Below, we describe our task generation pipelines organized by capability, followed by how we ensure the quality of the training trajectories. (cid:17) Behaviors before correctness Much of the data we used is unverified. We think it still teaches useful behavioral patterns, such as exploring repository, planning, and recovering from errors. Throughout mid-training and SFT, we trained on all trajectories, with only occasional correctness filtering, and replayed the correct ones during the final training phase. 10https://keenable.ai/

sections.title:
5.1 PRism Data Processing
We construct a corpus of GitHub pull requests (PRs) that combines development discussions with the
corresponding code changes and repository context. The pipeline comprises three components: PRism-
curator reconstructs and filters PR records, PRism-annotator adds structured semantic labels,
and PRism-synthesis transforms the resulting data into synthetic reasoning documents, coding tasks,
executable tasks for reinforcement learning, and multi-turn agent trajectories. This section describes
curation and annotation; synthesis is covered separately. Figure 17 summarizes the data flow.
sections.content: Figure 17: Overview of PRism data processing. Curation combines archived events with repository code, and annotation adds semantic labels. The resulting corpus provides inputs for five synthesis branches. The prism is schematic; band widths are not to scale.

sections.title:
5.2 PRism Data Curation
Event collection and reconstruction. We process GitHub Archive events and retain information relevant
to PRs, including PR updates, comments, reviews, pushes, and continuous integration events. Events
are normalized and partitioned by repository identifier for parallel processing. We then group records by
repository identifier and PR number, associating discussions and related events through PR references
and commit identifiers. Each reconstructed record preserves the PR metadata, participants, available
description revisions, and associated events.
sections.content: Selection criteria. We retain merged PRs targeting the main or master branch, with descriptions longer than ten characters after whitespace removal and changes to between one and fifteen files. PR descriptions may contain at most one distinct issue-style reference of the form #123. keyword filter excludes PRs whose titles or descriptions indicate dependency or version updates. We also require an identifiable landed commit, obtained from the recorded merge commit or inferred from push events. These criteria select changes with bounded scope and accompanying textual context. Code enrichment. For each retained PR, we retrieve the repository history and resolve the base and head revisions. Where available, the merge base defines the starting revision for extracting the change. We 45 collect the combined diff, individual commit patches, changed file paths, repository file list, and pre-change contents of the affected files. Extraction is subject to configurable limits on file counts and content size; truncation and retrieval errors are recorded. The enriched records are stored in Parquet format, preserving the original PR fields and adding the extracted code context. This representation links the description and discussion of change to its implementation and initial repository state.

sections.title:
5.3 PRism Annotation
Annotation dimensions. We use a language model with a fixed rubric to annotate each PR along three
dimensions. The domain label identifies the principal technical area, such as data engineering, security, or
compiler development. Change attributes provide multiple labels for properties such as bug fixes, feature
additions, refactoring, and the inclusion of tests. The complexity label describes the predominant reasoning
requirement: knowledge of frameworks or conventions, multi-step logical reasoning, or recognition of a
subtle behavior or edge case. These categories describe the nature of the task rather than an ordinal
difficulty level.
sections.content: Evidence and label assignment. The annotation prompt includes PR metadata, discussion, repository information, and extracted code context. The rubric prioritizes code evidence, followed by PR text and labels, repository metadata, and discussion or continuous integration metadata. The model is instructed to score each candidate label against explicit criteria and return the selected labels, scores, and short rationales. Domain and complexity annotations allow NONE label when evidence is insufficient, while change attributes may be empty. The prompt also specifies consistency rules for conflicting attributes. Structured output and provenance. Annotations are generated through vLLM with temperature zero and JSON schema constraint. Long inputs are truncated to fit the available context, and the original and retained prompt lengths are recorded. PRs with code-retrieval errors remain in the dataset but are left unannotated. The output preserves all input columns and appends the annotations, parsing status, and prompt truncation metadata. The resulting corpus retains the source evidence alongside its semantic labels, supporting subsequent analysis and preparation of inputs for the synthesis pipelines. Example record. Figure 18 shows an abbreviated annotated PR record. The PR fixes game behavior and adds sound effects; its annotations identify both bug fixes and feature additions. The complexity label is NONE, indicating insufficient evidence for specific reasoning category.

sections.title:
5.4 Developer thoughts synthesis
PR data records the detailed history of a repository but not the reasoning behind each change. To mitigate
this gap, we turn human-written code changes into long-context agentic data in text format by asking an
LLM to synthesize only the missing thoughts, while all the code comes from the PR itself.
sections.content: Synthesis. We use about 21M curated PRs from 2020 to 2024 (5.2). For every PR, we show its metadata, discussion, files before the change, and commit diffs to Qwen3.5-397B-A17B (Qwen Team, 2026) and ask it to write three kinds of prose: task description, the developers reasoning before each commit (or before each file within commit), and closing summary. We skip PRs with code-retrieval errors or whose prompt would exceed 32k tokens. We then splice the prose around the real repository tree, files before the change, and commit diffs. The result reads like an agentic coding session in text format: task, the relevant files, and sequence of reasoning steps, each followed by an actual code edit. All code in the document is real; only the thoughts are synthetic. 46 repo_id: 847236596 pr_number: 33 pull_request: title: "Fix: qol" merged: true base.ref: main changed_files: 8 commits: 6 code: repo_full_name: dice-2004/Union-Hack-2024 status: ok touched_files: [src/battle.py, src/enemy.py, ...] compare_diff: --- a/src/battle.py +++ b/src/battle.py ... - + pl.lvup_check() pl.lvup_check(sounds) annotation: domain.label: GAMES_SIMULATION_MISC_CRAFT attributes.labels: [BUGFIX, FEATURE_ADD] complexity.label: NONE prompt_was_truncated: false Figure 18: Abbreviated annotated PR record. Selected fields are shown in compact notation; ellipses mark omitted paths and diff context. Full records also contain base files, commit patches, events, annotation scores, and rationales. Diversity knobs. Applying single prompt and single document template to millions of PRs would produce highly repetitive data. We therefore draw knobs for every PR that control both what the LLM writes and how the final document is rendered. Prompt knobs set the style of the task description (GitHub issue, direct instruction, conversational, or specification), its level of detail, whether it includes plan or names the files to change, and whether reasoning is written per commit or per file. Rendering knobs set the diff format (unified, search/replace, or full file), what is shown at the end (combined diff, files after the change, or both), line numbers and their style, how files are delimited, truncation of long files, whether files are shown upfront or right before the commit that touches them, whether and how the repository tree is shown, where the repository is mentioned, and the connector phrases between sections. Since rendering knobs are applied after generation, the same LLM output can be turned into many different documents. Long context. Documents over 128k tokens are re-rendered more compactly (no files after the change, harder truncation of long files), and documents over 512k tokens are dropped. The resulting 14.6M documents (181B tokens) cover wide range of lengths: 8.8M documents are under 8k tokens, while over 1M documents are between 32k and 512k tokens.

sections.title:
5.5 PRism task synthesis
PRs are a natural source of realistic coding tasks for agents. We turn curated PRs into standalone tasks
that can be solved on the repository before the change, wrap them into instructions for a coding agent,
and collect agent trajectories solving them.
sections.content: Task synthesis. Starting from the curated PRs (5.2), we give GPT-OSS-120B with high reasoning effort (Agarwal et al., 2025) the PR metadata, commit subjects, combined diff, files before the change, and, optionally, the discussion comments, and ask it to write the task that the PR solves as an independent assignment, without referencing the PR or its diff. We skip PRs whose touched files exceed 5,000 lines 47 in total, as well as prompts over 32k tokens. The task is then combined with general instructions for an agent working in the repository, including language-specific setup hints based on the primary programming language of the repository. Difficulty control. We do not verify the solutions produced by agents on these tasks, so controlling task difficulty is important: tasks that are too hard are likely to result in incorrect solutions, while tasks that are too easy teach little. The main knob here is the amount of hints, with five levels: bare (a oneto three-sentence request, as typed in chat), concise (a title and short description), standard (adds pointers to environment setup files and high-level plan), guided (adds step-by-step plan and testing hints), and detailed (adds pointers to the files, functions, and design decisions). We sample the level based on the size of the PR, measured by the number of commits, diff lines, and touched files. Small PRs mostly get few hints (bare or concise 65% of the time), while large PRs mostly get many (guided or detailed 65% of the time). Every level appears at every PR size, but overall the distribution is biased towards balancing difficulty: large changes become more approachable with more guidance, while small changes stay realistic and underspecified. The agent instructions follow the opposite pattern: the fewer hints task contains, the more detailed the instructions and the stricter the requested verification. Diversity knobs. Other knobs vary the style of the task (direct instruction, GitHub issue, or specification), the persona (direct request or project maintainer guiding contributor), the scope (the minimal targeted change or open to restructuring related code), whether the PR discussion is shown to the LLM, and how the task is rendered (Markdown, plain text, or conversational, with varied headers, separators, and section names). The agent instructions vary in verbosity, workflow (phases, checklist, or free-form), verification strictness, guidance on honestly reporting problems, and response format. Agent trajectories. We run Qwen3.5-397B-A17B with thinking (Qwen Team, 2026) in the OpenCode agent harness on the synthesized tasks, each in sandbox with the repository at its state before the change. The agent explores the repository, sets up the environment, edits code, and runs tests using tools such as bash, read, and edit. The resulting 2.3M trajectories (70B tokens) are used in mid-training. (cid:17) Dont forget sandbox diversity We put lot of effort into task diversity but overlooked the sandboxes: in every trajectory, the repository was located at /workspace. The model learned this too well. In evaluations where the repository was elsewhere, it kept looking for /workspace; tasks that did not state the working directory took twice as many commands, and the pass rate fell by 40%. Starting from the fourth mid-training stage, we use an augmented version of the trajectories with varied working directories and programmatically inserted turn imitating an agent checking where it is.

sections.title:
5.6 PRism RL task synthesis
We use the same PR corpus as mentioned in §5.2 to create agentic coding tasks for RL training. Each task
needs an environment in which the agent’s solution can be run and verified. To build them, we filter the
corpus, rewrite each remaining PR into a task, synthesize an environment for it, and filter the environments
with a judge that inspects solver trajectories (Figure 19).
sections.content: Task design. task has four parts: the repository at the commit before the PR, an instruction that describes the change without revealing the solution, sandbox in which the projects tests run, and verifier that decides whether the agent succeeded. The PR also gives us reference solution (fix patch) 48 instruction / verifier rewrite Annotated GitHub PRs 1. Task filtering 2. Task rewrite synthesis 3. Environment synthesis Rule filters trivial, bot, forked, oversized, low-star LLM judge 8 dimensions, 03 quality, complexity Domain-balanced sample: easy / medium / hard Diff classification (no model) fix and test patches Task specification title, description, acceptance criteria Pinned blobless clone history scrubbed Runtime, eval.sh, Dockerfile u 6 1 u , p refiner strips leaks Container image Acceptance fail-to-pass inside the built image, verifier-hacking checklist, test-analyst alignment audit 64,000 validated Trajectory judge solver run scored on 5 dimensions deducted against an 18-pattern taxonomy keep 38,000 environments for agentic code RL binary reward Figure 19: Building RL coding environments from GitHub pull requests. Filtering reduces the annotated PR corpus with deterministic rules, then scores survivors with an LLM judge and draws domain-balanced sample stratified by difficulty. Rewriting derives the reference patches from the diff without model and uses the model only for the task specification, the predicted environment, and the test commands. Environment synthesis is an agent loop that produces container image. The two checks below it are distinct: acceptance is mechanical, whereas the trajectory judge runs solver against an already-accepted environment and decides whether it is worth training on. Solid arrows carry artifacts and dashed arrows carry feedback: acceptance failures return to the responsible sub-agent, and judged misalignment returns to the rewrite stage. Filter thresholds, the eight scoring dimensions of the filtering judge, the checklist items, and the selection rule are given in the text. which we use to check the verifier but never show to the agent. good task needs verifier that fails on the original code and passes with the reference solution. The task also has to be solvable, so that failed attempt reflects its difficulty rather than broken environment. The first property can be checked deterministically; the second needs an LLM judge and static checks. Task filtering and rewriting. Most PRs cannot be turned into usable task, so we drop PRs annotated as documentation-only, version bumps, reformatting, code regeneration, or refactoring, unless they also contain functional change. We also drop bot PRs, diffs over 200k characters, binary-only diffs, PRs against forks, PR bodies under 100 characters, and repositories with fewer than six stars or no package manifest. GPT-OSS-120B (Agarwal et al., 2025) then scores the remaining PRs on eight dimensions, and the quality score weights content strength 0.60 and environment feasibility 0.40. Finally, we sample task set balanced across 17 domains and label each PR as easy, medium, or hard relative to PRs with the same star bucket, domain, and language. merged PR already contains its answer, so we rewrite it into specification of what to implement, with the level of detail set by the difficulty knobs. The reference patches come directly from the diff against the merge base which we split by file into fix_patch and test_patch. An LLM writes the title, description, acceptance criteria, and test commands, and second pass compares the draft with the test patch to remove identifiers leaked from the fix and claims the tests do not check. 49 (cid:17) Diff against the merge base The base commit recorded on PR is not always the commit the change was written against. The commit that matches the diff is the merge base, the common ancestor of the PRs base and head branches. The two differ in about 15% of PRs because of branch drift. Environment synthesis. task also needs an environment to run and verifier we can trust. An agent using the OpenCode harness based on Qwen3.5-397B-A17B (Qwen Team, 2026) builds both, delegating to sub-agents that explore the repository, set up the runtime, write and audit the evaluation script, and build the Dockerfile. It works in blobless clone at the merge base with all git history and references removed. It installs dependencies with the projects own package manager and checks with dry run that the tests can be collected; it has at most 16 turns to finish. Hidden tests stay outside the working tree. An environment is accepted only if it is fail-to-pass: the evaluation script fails on the original repository and passes with the reference patch applied, both run inside the built image. Because the same agent writes the environment and its verifier, test-analyst sub-agent and static checks audit the verifier before acceptance. Accepted environments are exported in Harbor format (task.toml, instruction.md, environment/, tests/, and solution/) with binary reward. Judge filtering. Passing fail-to-pass does not mean that task is useful for training. We therefore run solver on each accepted environment and judge its trajectory on five dimensions, including environment readiness, dependency completeness, and verifier integrity. The judge first identifies which of 18 failure patterns occur (e.g., runtime that never starts, missing package, tests that never run, or solver that searches without editing), and lowers dimensions score only when it has identified matching pattern. deterministic rule then maps the scores to quality buckets like keep, downweight, or reject. When the judge flags mismatch between the instruction and the verifier, we repair the task instead of discarding it: faulty verifier is realigned with the instruction, and an unclear instruction is rewritten from the solver trajectory, with up to two candidates that are checked for leakage and accepted only if new solver run scores higher. With this approach, we created roughly 64k environments that passed validation, of which 38k were rated high quality and used for RL training. (cid:17) Watch out for verifier hacking When an agent writes both the environment and the grader, passing fail-to-pass tests becomes deceptively easy. script that exits 0 is much cheaper to write than one that runs real test suite, and the synthesis agent often took that shortcut in our initial runs. We therefore added regex checks that catch verifiers that only check that the patch files exist instead of running tests, grepping the reference patches, using git diff as an oracle, or throwing away the test commands exit code. Agents get around these static checks with inline scripts and custom commands. We therefore add test-analyst LLM judge that reads the verifier source and its execution trace. It checks that the script calls recognized test runner and its result comes from real assertions, and that it gives different results on the clean and the patched tree.

sections.title:
5.7 Subagent delegation
Long coding tasks require an agent to spend context on repository exploration, file contents, command
output, and test results. To study whether delegation can improve this process, we collect trajectories
in which a parent agent may assign one bounded piece of work to a child agent. Each child runs in a
sections.content: 50 fresh OpenCode session and returns final report to the parent, which then checks the report and decides whether to use it. The complete parent and child sessions are retained separately. Tasks. We start from Harbor coding environments derived from merged pull requests. The original sandbox and verifier are left unchanged. Kimi K3 is used for task-instruction synthesis. Given digest of the original change, it writes short description of the required behavior, the shared interface between the workstreams, and several pieces of work that can be developed and checked independently. fixed template then asks the solver to validate these workstreams and integrate the result before finishing. The instruction synthesizer produces prose only. We reject drafts that mention files from the reference patch, copy patch text, or explicitly instruct the solver to delegate or use subagents. This results in 908 tasks. Rollouts. We run Kimi K3 with thinking enabled at maximum reasoning effort in the OpenCode harness (Anomaly, 2026), orchestrated by our rollout engine, with Harbor executing the sandbox and verifier. The parent agent has the usual repository tools and task tool that can launch one of two specialists in fresh context. The investigator traces repository behavior and answers focused question; the implementer performs one bounded change. The parent prompt describes these roles and asks the parent to verify load-bearing details in childs report before relying on them. Delegation is optional: the task instruction does not require child call, and recursive delegation is disabled. Parent and child tool calls are executed within the same Harbor task environment, while their OpenCode sessions and trajectories remain separate. We retain valid four-hour rollouts together with eight additional valid trials from the two-hour run. Of the 908 tasks, 850 produced at least one valid trajectory, while 58 failed both attempts. Harbor evaluates each trial with the original task verifier. Training records. Each parent and child session is serialized as separate training trajectory. The parent trajectory contains the task call and the report returned by the child; the child document preserves the detailed work performed in the child session. trial whose Harbor verifier returns reward 1 is labeled correct. Child labels are inherited from the parent trial and therefore are parent-level labels rather than independent child-verifier judgments. The four sources then pass through the shared SFT validator (5.17). Correct documents allow five consecutive tool errors, while other documents allow three. The resulting collection contains 3,041 documents and 131.6M tokens  (Table 18)  . Source Documents Tokens Parent, verified Parent, other Child, parent-verified Child, parent-other 618 290 1,349 784 45.5M 21.6M 37.9M 26.5M 3,041 Total

sections.title:
5.8 SWE Efficiency
Our SWE Efficiency pipeline, inspired by Ma et al.
(2025), transforms real-world, performance-oriented
pull requests into reproducible optimization tasks and
agentic engineering trajectories. Curation identifies
suitable changes, prepares executable environments,
and establishes correctness checks and representative performance workloads. During generation, coding
agents investigate the repository, analyze behavioral invariants and compatibility requirements, develop
optimizations, and iteratively validate their changes through tool execution and feedback. The emphasis
is on evidence-grounded engineering: proposed improvements must preserve required behavior, and
performance claims must be supported by measurements. We retain interaction histories and execution
evidence to enable traceability, quality assessment, and subsequent auditing. Reviews consider functional
sections.content: Table 18: Parent and child trajectories retained for SFT. Child labels are inherited from the parent trials verifier outcome, not from independent child-level judgments. 131.6M 51 correctness, measured performance, and consistency between the agents explanations and observed results, with accepted trajectories maintained separately from lower-confidence records. With this pipeline, we synthesized 700 SFT-format agentic traces.

sections.title:
5.9 File Manipulation
We built two pipelines producing teacher trajectories for office work with files such as spreadsheets, docu-
ments, slide decks, PDFs, HTML pages and technical drawings. They are inspired by GDPval (Patwardhan
et al., 2025). A task consists of optional input files and an instruction, usually an e-mail from a manager
or colleague or an assignment brief, that asks for one or more files to be created or edited, or for a written
answer drawn from the input files.
sections.content: Both pipelines start each task from real files. They differ in where the files come from: the first collects public documents from the web (5.9.1), and the second mines office files from the repositories of our PR dataset (5.9.2).

sections.title: 5.9.1 Tasks from Public Documents
sections.content: Figure 20: File manipulation pipeline from public documents. Source files are found by web searches over sectors and occupations, then crawled and filtered. Each task combines an input package, task family and sampled plan, from which an LLM writes the request. Teacher models solve the tasks in two harnesses, with randomized environment and, in some rollouts, simulated user. Source files. The source files are pool of documents scraped from public sources. We used 18 NAICS sectors and 89 O*NET occupations that form superset of those included in GDPval. We then create search queries and use them to find domains that would publish documents related to each sector/occupation (e.g., trucking association publishing freight rate tables). We then crawled such domains for files with office-like extensions (e.g., pptx, xlsx, docx, and pdf). After basic filtering and deduplication, we used Qwen3.6-27B model to score each file across 6 weighted criteria, including whether the file could be the input of realistic professional task and how well it fits the selected sectors and occupations. The same model also extracts metadata (identifiers such as case numbers, entities such as project names, organizations, and topics from generated taxonomy), which we use to group related files into multi-file packages. Finally, we use the scores to filter files based on threshold, leaving approximately 115k files.

sections.title: File type
sections.content: pdf xlsx docx pptx CAD (STEP) Other (HTML, XML, CSV, plain text)

sections.title: Share
sections.content: 66,395 19,597 12,872 3,596 2,300 10,240 57.7% 17.0% 11.2% 3.1% 2.0% 8.9% 115,000 100% Table 19: Public files used as seeds, by file type. Task synthesis. We roughly follow these four steps to synthesize task from the pool of documents. First, we sample an input package containing either single, multiple, or no files. Second, we sample plan along the diversity dimensions described below. Third, an agent using DeepSeek-V4-Flash receives this plan and the input package to produce plain-prose request written as an internal memo addressed to worker mentioning the situation, the inputs and sentence listing every file to be delivered. We then create task folder with the input package, the generated request and the drawn plan. To diversify the tasks, we sample each plan along the following dimensions: Deliverable: the file format and the number of files. Kind of work: produce, analyze, decide, verify or transform. Complexity: the reasoning depth and the quantitative level. External research: how much outside research the task needs. Context: the stakes, the audience and the register of the request. Occupation and sector: drawn from list of 358 titles, favoring under-covered sectors. Style: how the request opens, the kind of employer, and naming tradition for any people in it. Each task also belongs to one of five families. No-file, single-file, and multi-file tasks come with zero, one, or several input files. Technical-drawing tasks list physical inventory in full (e.g., equipment, rooms, or wiring) and ask for plan, schematic, or layout as PDF, optionally with SVG or STEP files. Numerical-reconciliation tasks ask for named values such as totals, variances, or converted amounts, computed from 36 figures that code extracts from the input file or places in the request. Each values direction, unit, and rounding are stated so that it has exactly one correct answer. Teacher rollouts. We solve the tasks with several teacher models, including Kimi K3/2.6 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, in different agent harnesses, such as OpenCode and Stirrup, the open-source harness behind GDPval-AA. We also randomize the environment of each rollout: the system prompt is rewritten or paraphrased, the workspace path, the user name, and the tool and argument names vary across trajectories, and some rollouts give the teacher set of office-file skills. In some rollouts, model plays the user and sends follow-up requests, so the teacher must revise its work over several turns. Teacher Traj. Tokens Kimi K2.6 Kimi K3 DeepSeek-V4-Flash 63.6k 220.0k 45.6k 3.5B 17.7B 7.0B Total 329.2k 28.2B Table 20: Trajectories and tokens per teacher model.

sections.title: 5.9.2 Tasks from Repository Files
sections.content: Figure 21: File manipulation pipeline from GitHub repositories: from file to task. Source files. We mine input files from the repositories of our PR dataset (5.2), which yields 1.3M office files (PDF, Word, Excel and PowerPoint) across 85k repositories. An agent downloads each file and matches it against taxonomy of 57 work meta-templates grounded on O*NET occupations. Each template describes cluster of economically valuable office tasks and the input files they need. Of the 1.29M files we downloaded and the 1.08M we classified, 254k (23.6%) match at least one meta-template, giving 269k filetemplate pairs, of which 170,520 became tasks. Task synthesis. The main objective during task synthesis was to create distribution as wide as possible while keeping economically valuable office work at its center. To achieve this, we split task synthesis into two agent runs: one designs the task, and the other writes it. To avoid diversity collapse on each step we anchor the agents with long form description files that avoid details and examples, and we use an external sampler to draw an instantiation of variety of knobs proposed by the agents themselves. The anchors are two manifold documents, long prose files generated from representative set of economically valuable tasks. They describe office work at the population level and contain no example tasks or details. The first, real-work manifold, describes how real tasks vary: how the deliverable relates to the input files, how much of the answer is already in the inputs and how much must be constructed, where ambiguity lives, and whether multiple inputs agree or conflict. The second, artifact-shape manifold, describes what requests and files look like, from how managers phrase instructions to the operational mess of real files. We used Kimi K2.6 for both agent runs. In the design run, the agent receives the source file, the metatemplate, the real-work manifold and proposes design space: the axes along which task built from this file could vary, where we encourage behavioral diversity over cosmetic diversity. An external sampler is used to draw an instantiation from the proposed design space, so the agent defines the support but does not choose the draw (Gu et al., 2026). With the draw, the agent then writes brief describing what the draw means for this file. In the writing run, new agent reads the file, the meta-template, the design brief and the artifact-shape manifold, and creates the task. Synthesized tasks take the shape of managers e-mail plus the agents starting workspace: the source file (potentially modified) and, in third of the tasks, synthesized companion files to create multi-file tasks. 54 Teacher rollouts. We solve each synthesized task once with Kimi K2.6 in our fork of the forge harness. Before the rollout, for 95% of the tasks, short-lived agent proposes several system-prompt styles, an external sampler picks one, and the agent then writes the system prompt in that style. We also include the traces from the task synthesis stage as part of the training corpus. Table 21 summarizes the counts created from this pipeline.

sections.title:
5.10.1 Open-ended research conversations
Many search requests have no single short answer: a user wants to understand a topic, compare options, or
see how something works, and expects an account assembled from several sources. To teach this behavior,
we generated multi-turn research conversations in which an agent searches our pre-training corpus through
Search360 (§5.10), reads documents, and writes an answer grounded in what it found. We call this data
Agentic Semantic Packing: length-controlled, search-grounded conversations with tool calls.14
sections.content: Queries. We started from the 1.01M training queries of MS MARCO (Nguyen et al., 2016) and asked an LLM to rewrite 565k of them (good candidates for deep research) in five directions: follow-up about consequences, more specific question, comparison with related concept, question about the underlying mechanism, and question about practical application. This gave 3.83M queries, which we split into disjoint sets, one per target length, so that no query appears at two lengths. Target length Trajectories Tokens Agent. The agent runs ReAct loop with two tools: search, which returns the top five passages with their document IDs, and get_document, which returns full document truncated to 30k characters. Results with low relevance scores are kept but marked with note suggesting other search terms, rather than silently dropped. Before call is executed, validator rejects repeated queries, near-duplicates of earlier queries (word Jaccard similarity of at least 0.85), and documents that were already read, and returns the reason, so the trace shows the agent trying different angle instead of looping. Each conversation samples user persona along four axes with six values each: role (e.g., expert researcher, curious student, skeptical reviewer), interaction style (e.g., formal, Socratic, time-pressed), behavioral Table 22: Search-based research conversations used in mid-training, by target length. 1,322k 436k 80k 38.1B 47.2B 30.8B 32k 128k 512k 116.1B 1,838k Total 11https://github.com/LLM360/forgecode/tree/981e7ac35d31d03690156d76a3850f526e75a737, the commit pinned in the release. 12https://github.com/LLM360/cowbox 13https://github.com/ifm-ai/file-manipulation-pipeline 14https://github.com/ifm-ai/agentic_semantic_packing 55 trait (e.g., concise, detail-oriented, big-picture), and research approach (e.g., depth-first, hypothesis-driven, comparative), for 1,296 combinations. The persona shapes both the system prompt and the wording of the user turns. Between research steps, simulated user writes follow-up messages that refer to specific findings the agent has reported, and occasional nudges (to read full document, reflect on what has been learned, or rephrase failed search) are drawn from pools that include the option to say nothing. Each conversation runs until it reaches target length and ends with consolidation of the key findings and final synthesis (5.16.2). Filtering. We converted the traces to chat format with tool definitions and removed those with leftover special tokens or channel markers, malformed role sequences, or lengths over budget. second filter removed traces with garbled tokens (stray non-Latin characters in English prose), empty assistant turns alongside tool calls, refusals, and tool-call markup leaking into assistant text. In our largest generation run, 668,591 of 673,040 traces (99.3%) passed these checks. Data. We used the conversations in mid-training. They comprise 1.84M trajectories with 116B tokens at three target lengths up to 512k tokens  (Table 22)  .

sections.title:
5.10.2 Multi-hop complex search data
A portion of our search tasks is generated by an automated synthesis pipeline over a local Wikipedia
snapshot. Inspired by Gao et al. (2025), we use an e5-base-v2 encoder and a FAISS index of approximately
26 million Wikipedia passages for dense retrieval. We retain only questions that can be answered through
the same retriever interface later available to the agent. We first compile the snapshot’s inter-article
links into an entity graph, then sample multi-hop chains by walking it, biasing each hop towards a more
widely linked entity so that the walk terminates at a recognizable anchor. Each edge of a sampled chain is
grounded before it is used: we fetch the source article, locate the passage that mentions the next entity,
and extract the relation together with a supporting quotation from that passage, so no relation is proposed
by a model out of context, and a chain is discarded outright if any one of its edges cannot be grounded this
way. The chain is then composed into a question in reverse, from the anchor towards the hidden answer,
with every intermediate entity referred to only by its relation to the preceding one, which forces the chain
to be resolved sequentially rather than in parallel.
sections.content: Two further stages harden the item. The first enforces answer uniqueness: we enumerate the entities that satisfy the final relation. Where more than one does, we add attributes that hold for the intended answer and no alternative, while each remaining generic enough to describe many other entities, so the question is pinned down without becoming fingerprint of its answer. The second replaces the name of each intermediate entity with description assembled from facts taken from that entitys own article, under validator that rejects any rewrite in which the name survives. Difficulty is then set by two independent knobs: the number of hops and the number of entities so described. We synthesize five bands, from two hops with no obfuscated entities to six hops with four obfuscated entities, allocating progressively more items to the harder bands. Finally, every candidate passes two-sided difficulty gate, measured rather than assumed. It is discarded unless strong model answering from parametric memory alone fails all eight attempts, which establishes that retrieval is necessary, and an agent given the retriever succeeds at least once in eight independent trials while its success rate over the first four trials stays below per-band ceiling, establishing that the item is solvable but not easy. Items that survive are annotated with the number of tool calls their successful solutions required.

sections.title:
5.11 Tool use
General tool-use data synthesis. To supplement scarce real agentic data, we built a fully automated
pipeline that turns a bare domain name (e.g., flight booking, incident triage) into an executable environment
sections.content: 56 together with verified multi-step tasks. For each domain, model first designs relational SQLite schema and populates it layer by layer along foreign-key topology, then writes Python tool API over that world, so that the agent sees only function signatures and never SQL. The tools are analyzed into tool-dependency graph whose edges encode data flow (one tools return field feeds anothers required parameter) and state dependency, and tasks are sampled as paths through this graph rather than written free-form, which makes hallucinated tool names and unsatisfiable calls structurally impossible. Each sampled chain is rendered into an executable reference solution. The initial database state is reverse-constructed so that the chain is feasible by design, distractor entities are injected, and model jointly writes the natural-language instruction and programmatic verifier. Every candidate must then survive triple-check (the solution runs, the verifier accepts the post-state, and the verifier rejects the initial state), battery of deterministic static guards covering invented literals, instruction-to-verifier literal coverage, chain-order consistency and untouched-row negative checks, rubric-based QC review, and finally pass@k rollout filter that discards unsolvable items and parks each task at its solvable difficulty frontier. O*NET-grounded tool-use data synthesis. To ground tool-use data in economically meaningful work, we adapt the scenario generator of Somerstep et al. (2026), which turns O*NET occupational tasks into tool-mediated workplace requests (Figure 22). The tool ecosystem is built from the Smithery registry of Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers: we crawl every listed server, have an LLM write an analysis of its purpose and tools, and keep servers an agent can connect to without enterprise purchases or private API keys, then probe each tool with realistic inputs and retain those that return real, non-error data. Each O*NET task is matched to the servers most likely to help accomplish it by embedding the task statement and the server analyses with Qwen3 embedding model and thresholding their cosine similarity. scenario is generated from an occupation together with several matched (task, server) pairs: the generator LLM is given the occupation and task descriptions, web search results about them to supply realistic constraints and context, and the servers tool schemas. It then writes self-contained workplace request that needs minimum number of tools across more than one server to complete, cross-tool workflow whose links are labeled by dependency type (parameter dependency, conditional routing, cross-validation, or aggregation), and an answer key of the required tool calls with schema-conformant arguments and expected outputs. The request must contain every concrete value the agent needs (IDs, names, dates, and so on), must not name the tools or servers, and must not be answerable without calling tools. For multi-turn data, we also generate information-withheld variants that leave out one to three key parameters, so the agent has to ask clarifying questions. simulated user answers them via role inversion: it runs in its own session, where it believes it is the assistant, receives the agents replies as user messages, and never sees the agents reasoning or tool calls. Because live MCP servers are rate-limited and unstable at scale, rollouts use virtual tools: an LLM that sees the server and tool documentation, the input schema and the running simulation history returns realistic tool outputs, after checking that required arguments are present, no hallucinated arguments were passed, and argument types match the schema. The resulting singleand multi-turn trajectories are used as mid-training data. Automatic pipeline for skill-use data synthesis. Skills equip LLM agents with professional knowledge and guidance to complete long-horizon and complex tasks. To teach and improve LLMs skill-use capability, we start from public skills, and use an automatic pipeline to construct tasks where skills provide advantages in completion. We first crawl 184k skills from GitHub and skills.sh, deduplicate and filter them. Around 12k skills that are complete, clearly written, and executable offline in container are kept. Then, we use builder-reviewer agentic pipeline to build tasks. The pipeline first writes initial Docker files for skills, where basic dependencies are installed. Then, starting with these initial environments, the builder is instructed to build multiple types of tasks, including multi-hop, abductive diagnosis, constraint satisfaction, and 57 Figure 22: O*NET-grounded tool-use data synthesis, adapted from Somerstep et al. (2026). The tool ecosystem keeps only Smithery MCP servers that an agent can reach and whose tools return real data. Each O*NET task is matched to servers by embedding similarity, and an occupation with several matched (task, server) pairs is expanded by an LLM into self-contained workplace request, cross-tool workflow and an answer key; information-withheld variants (dashed) omit key parameters so the agent must ask for them. Rollouts run against LLM-simulated tools and, for multi-turn data, role-inverted simulated user that sees only the agents final replies. partial-ordering. Each type is based on one profile, specifying the detailed steps for building such tasks. For example, multi-hop asks the builder to explore the workspace step-by-step and form the corresponding task with these sequential steps, where the input of one step is the output of the previous. Details of the other task types are in Wang et al. (2026). Each task comes with an instruction, verifier, and corresponding solution. The pipeline produced skill-related tasks at large scale. Skill-driven tool-use data synthesis. Skills provide general-purpose agents with procedural guidance for specialized tasks, including when and how to use tools (Zhang et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2026b). In this pipeline we view skills as examples of realistic LLM uses and synthesize corresponding tasks. Given selected set of skills, we construct an environment supporting their tools and workflows, then generate contextualized tasks that require agents to apply them. The previous pipeline gives the agent skill and builds tasks where using it helps. This pipeline treats skills as descriptions of real workflows and builds tasks that require carrying out those workflows, with or without the skill file. We collected approximately 400k skill records from sources such as GitHub and ClawHub, normalized them, removed exact and near-duplicates (via MinHash LSH), and translated non-English skills, yielding approximately 160k skills. Each skill is annotated with domain, capability, and quality to guide sampling 58 toward under-represented domains and high-quality workflows, and we construct directed skill graph based on inputoutput compatibility (Fan et al., 2026) so that subgraphs of complementary skills can be composed into more complex workflows. For each sampled skill (or subgraph), an LLM derives representative workflow specifying each steps inputs, outputs, and required tools; an LLM with harness then produces executable tool simulations and materializes the data they operate on, using web search to ground textual and structured data in public sources, media generators, and document renderers to produce artifacts such as images, videos, and PDFs. Finally, given the workflow and generated data, the agent curates contextualized task with instructions, deliverables, an oracle solution, and verification scripts, which we package with the simulated tools and initial environment state to form complete task instance. (cid:17) Skills are noisy and stateless Skill files are diverse but noisy: sampling them at random or by embedding similarity yields largely incompatible combinations. The graph greatly helps yield coherent and composable workflows. They also carry no state or data, and LLMs asked to simulate it directly produce one-line, simplistic states; grounding generation in external tools such as web search yields richer, higher-quality states.

sections.title:
5.12.1 Task factory
Question–answer sites and papers contain many hard, checkable science problems, but a problem is not yet
a training environment. Reinforcement learning needs a sandbox, a deliverable the agent must produce, a
verifier whose reward can be trusted, and some knowledge of how hard the task is. We built a task factory15
that turns candidate problems into Harbor tasks, each with an instruction, a container environment, a
programmatic verifier, and a reference solution that the verifier accepts, each audited for reward hacking and
calibrated against a real agent. The factory is itself an agent program in the spirit of autoresearch (Karpathy,
2026): a Markdown file that a coding agent receives as its instructions, together with a small set of skills for
the individual checks, and that it follows in a loop without supervision (Figure 23). Several of us ran it in
parallel campaigns over Stack Exchange and arXiv, and it produced 9,220 tasks from 15 sources (Table 23).
Every task was audited with the gates that reinforcement learning needs: verifier probes, a reward-hacking
audit, and review by a second model.
sections.content: The loop. For each task, the agent reads an append-only ledger of previous attempts to find under-covered areas and recurring failures, mines candidate problems from the source, and picks one with finite, checkable answer; proofs, opinions, and prose answers are rejected. It computes the answer with script before writing any assertion, writes the task, and runs the reference solution through the verifier, abandoning the task after three failed attempts. It then calibrates the task with pass@4 against an open model and triages every trial into failure class, such as correct answer rejected by the verifier, an ambiguous instruction, timeout, loop, or tooling error. Patterns across trials are read as evidence about the task rather than the agent: if every trial misreads the same clause, the instruction is ambiguous; if every trial gives the same wrong answer, the verifier may be wrong; if every passing trial brute-forced, the task is easy whatever its score. An ambiguous instruction or wrong verifier is fixed and recalibrated once; genuine difficulty is kept, and infrastructure failures are never counted as difficulty. Tasks are published with difficulty label from their pass rate, and overall 65% of the tasks are labeled hard, 31% medium, and 4% easy. When several agents mined the same source in parallel, they converged on the same few problem 15https://github.com/ifm-ai/task-factory 59 Figure 23: Task factory. coding agent runs this loop without supervision: it finds problem with checkable answer, grounds it as Harbor task, passes it through three gates that are never skipped, measures its difficulty against real agent, and logs every attempt, pass or fail, to ledger that it reads before building the next task. types; in materials science, for example, most tasks drifted toward elastic tensors and Debye temperatures until we assigned each agent its own subfield. Grounding rules. few rules each cost us tasks before they were written down. The instruction never names its source, since an agent will look it up. The reference solution and the verifier share no derivation code, and third, independent check substitutes the expected answer back into the original problem: when the same wrong formula appears on both sides, the oracle passes while correct agents fail (a concordant bug; see the box below). The verifier follows an output contract under which capable agent that follows the instruction always receives reward 1: it parses JSON, compares numbers as numbers, and ignores order where order carries no meaning. When correct answer is rejected, the instruction is fixed first and the format handling second, and the domain bar is never lowered. Gates for reinforcement learning. task that passes its oracle and scores 1/4 can still be useless for RL, so every task also passes three gates that are never skipped. The reference solution must pass. probe battery submits empty, wrong, malformed, truncated, and partially correct answers, and every one must score 0, since verifier that has only seen the reference answer has not been tested. reward-hacking audit then asks whether the agent can score 1 without doing the work: whether the verifier or expected answer is visible or reachable in the sandbox, whether ground truth is recomputed from files the agent can edit, and whether tests or the reward file are writable. second model with no shared context reviews each finished task for contamination, brute-forceability, ambiguity, and verifier fitness, since the agent that wrote task is the wrong one to judge it. Hardening the reward channel. The largest class of exploits we found was not in the tasks but in where they ran. The agent originally ran as root in the container in which the verifier ran afterwards, so it could replace the Python interpreter, write the reward file in advance, or leave process behind that rewrote the reward after grading. We now run the agent as an unprivileged user, and the verifier clears and seals the reward directory, stops leftover agent processes, and fails closed if any of these steps did not take effect; after this change, the class disappeared from later audits. second class of exploits came from verifiers 60 that graded finite sample of cases: lookup table with 25 entries, or fingerprint of seeded random generator, was enough to score 1. We added probe that replays memorized outputs, and the rule to grade the contract stated in the instruction rather than sample of it. Prohibitions in the instruction (do not use tool X) that the verifier did not check were bypassed as well, for example, with small wrapper that evaded lexical blocklist. Finally, some sandbox backends cannot close network access; on these backends, every contamination verdict is provisional, which is one more reason why instructions never name their source. What makes task hard. Across the first several hundred tasks, the separation was consistent. Agents solved tasks with small search space, closed-form answer, single library call, or textbook algorithm on small inputs. They failed tasks that combine several concepts, hinge on an edge case that the obvious approach gets wrong, require large structured output rather than single number, or need representation that cannot be brute-forced. We therefore preferred problems where the domain is hard rather than the code: domain expert with computer should solve them in minutes. (cid:17) 0/4 is claim about the task, not the agent task that no agent solves looks like the hard task we want, and it is also where broken verifier hides. When the reference solution and the verifier derive the answer the same way, shared mistake passes the oracle and rejects every correct answer; such concordant bugs were the leading cause of false 0/4 scores. real 0/4 looks different: on one materials-science task, all four trials converted GPa1 to TPa1 by dividing by 1000 instead of multiplying. We trust hard score only after an independent check substitutes the expected answer back into the original problem.

sections.title:
5.12.2 Creating Paper-Grounded Autoresearch Environments
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) (Kyars, 2026; Lambert et al., 2025) often trains
language models using a binary signal indicating whether an answer is correct or a task has been accomplished.
Many scientific and engineering objectives, however, are not simple binary tasks but are continuously
evaluated: a CUDA kernel can run faster, a material can become more conductive, and a numerical method
can achieve lower error or run faster. Progress on these problems depends on proposing new hypotheses,
testing their effects, and building on successful experiments. Recent systems like Autoresearch (Karpathy,
2026) illustrate the potential of language models in this setting. The Darwin Gödel Machine (Zhang et al.,
2026) extends this idea to agent self-improvement by modifying its own code and empirically evaluating
the resulting agents.
sections.content: 61 Paperrepository mining prompt Role. Identify paperrepository pairs that support short, substantive CPU experiment. Inputs. Assigned shard and window; paper and repository links; provenance flags; existing candidate notes; prior exclusions. Instructions. 1. Reconstruct the canonical queue: retain GitHub roots with at least one provenance signal; exclude known candidates; deduplicate and order using the specified hashes. Inspect only the assigned window. 2. Read the actual paper and inspect the linked repository. Verify that the code implements the stated contribution, rather than merely citing the paper. 3. Identify concrete executable slice of core method or meaningful ablation. Specify its entry point, smallest useful input, command, and expected output. Prefer bundled examples or small local fixtures. 4. Assess whether the complete experiment fits the CPU budget (approximately 510 minutes). Record measured runtime when tested and distinguish estimates from verified execution. 5. Reject paths requiring GPUs, large checkpoints or datasets, substantial training, or notebook-only execution. An import or packaging test alone is insufficient evidence of the core method. Return. For each retained candidate, write structured note with paper/repository links, contribution, runnable command, inputs, dependencies, runtime evidence, risks, and Pass/Borderline verdict. Return scan receipt with inspected/accepted/rejected counts, created-note paths, rejection reasons, and coverage status. Report no acceptance when evidence is insufficient; preserve prior notes and assigned shard boundaries. Figure 24: Condensed mining prompt. Queue construction is deterministic for fixed dataset and exclusion set; scientific and runtime feasibility are assessed from the paper and executable repository. Motivated by these approaches, we constructed autoresearch environments: each provides working baseline, and the task is to improve continuous metric over it. These environments aim to teach the scientific method of cycling through proposing hypotheses or changes, implementing them, measuring their effects, and retaining better solutions. We designed the environments to be solvable: there exists solution or change in the working environment that can produce an improvement or positive reward. We start from Paper with Code dataset, which contains 300,161 papercode links. We first mine it for candidates across machine learning, statistics, numerical methods, optimization, physics, and engineering, and scout each candidate to check that task can be solved under our time and resource limits (e.g., our sandboxes have no GPUs). In the mining phase, scouting agents inspect the actual paper and repository to verify their relationship and identify small executable slice of core contribution or meaningful ablation. We keep only candidates whose experiment runs within 510 minutes on CPU, and drop any that require GPUs, large checkpoints, large benchmark downloads, or substantial training. At the end of the mining phase, each scouting agent is asked to produce structured note for each retained candidate with links to the paper, repository, contributions from the paper that could potentially be turned into task, and related artifacts. We describe the mining prompt below in Figure 24. For each selected candidate, an environment construction agent reads the full paper and freezes the repository at commit. It identifies measurable objective, runnable baseline, and research insight from the paper that can guide improvement. The baseline may be published comparison method, repository ablation, or deliberately simplified implementation. Then, the agent packages the code, inputs, dependencies, instructions, evaluator, verifier, and reference solution as Harbor task. For each task, we generate three variants with varying difficulty levels of easy, medium, and hard, with different implementation scope or hints that the agent can use to solve the task. Each variant has an instruction.md 62 specifying the editable surface in the code, baseline metric, target metric, scoring direction, the reward formula, research hints, and the exact evaluation command. All essential requirements are available inside the task. The task begins with executable code and an observable baseline score so an agent can immediately enter hypothesisimplementevaluaterefine loop. We intentionally leave algorithmic choices open: alternative models, optimizers, search heuristics, numerical methods, kernels, or data transforms may improve the same objective. The research hint offers useful starting direction while leaving implementation and experimentation to the solver. Each task has 10-minute resource budget. Let b, t, and denote the measured baseline, target, and candidate metric. For valid candidate, the standard reward is R(m) = clip[0,1] clip[0,1] (cid:19) (cid:18) (cid:18) , higher is better, (cid:19) , lower is better. (13) After the tasks and their corresponding instructions are generated, the construction protocol first checks that the staged code and evaluator run under the actual container paths. Each variant is then executed with Harbors oracle agent, which applies the reference solution and runs the verifier. High oracle reward establishes that the task is indeed solvable and runs in the constructed environment, and if any task or environment failures are detected, they are repaired before model calibration. Model calibration is conducted to test for any tasks that are too easy or too hard for language model. For this calibration stage, the configured evaluation model runs four separate Harbor attempts from the staged task. Each attempt may experiment within its own budget, after which the verifier executes the resulting implementation and records its measured metric and normalized reward. We use mean@4 as the difficulty score. Finally, we review the trajectories under each of the rollouts to distinguish substantive model failures from ambiguous instructions, verifier defects, and environment problems.

sections.title:
5.12.3 Socratic style dialogue reasoning data generation
We created the synthetic reasoning datasets for chemistry and broader scientific domains using two
complementary sources: the Open Reaction Database (ORD)16 and MegaScience (Fan et al., 2025). We
transformed questions (direct QAs from the ORD and Megascience) derived from these sources into
Socratic student–teacher dialogues, capturing solution attempts over the iterations, targeted feedback, and
subsequent revisions as shown in Figure 25.
sections.content: ORD provides publicly available organic reaction records describing reactants, products, reaction conditions, experimental procedures, and measured outcomes. We constructed questionanswer pairs spanning six tasks: product prediction, retrosynthesis, condition prediction, yield prediction, procedure description, and reaction temperature prediction. We curated the resulting corpus by deduplicating reactions with identical reaction SMILES and retaining the most complete experimental record from each group, limiting repeated answers while selecting structurally diverse examples, and filtering questions containing unresolved compound references or extraction artifacts. MegaScience (Fan et al., 2025) complements the reaction-focused ORD data with scientific questions and reference answers spanning multiple disciplines. Its coverage includes chemistry, physics, biology, medicine, mathematics, computer science, and economics, providing broader foundation for scientific reasoning. 16https://open-reaction-database.org/about 63 Figure 25: Socratic dialogue data generation. student model attempts each question and teacher model with the reference answer guides it with hints until the answer is correct. Student turns become assistant outputs for SFT. For both sources, we generated dialogues using Qwen3.5-397B-A17B (Qwen Team, 2026) in student and teacher roles, with reasoning enabled for both. The student attempted to solve the question, while the teacher additionally received the reference answer and task-specific guidance. The teacher was instructed to guide the student through concise questions and hints, identify errors, and conclude the dialogue when it judged the response correct and complete. For supervised fine-tuning, we retained student reasoning and responses as assistant outputs and intermediate teacher feedback as user messages. After validation and length filtering, the final corpus contained 565,699 dialogues, comprising 372,831 from ORD and 192,868 from MegaScience.

sections.title:
5.12.4 Source grounded question synthesis
We started our source collection with a set of topics related to the benchmark relevant topics and relevant
to expert-level reasoning then expanded our search with adjacent topics. We expanded coverage in two
ways: large-scale web retrieval, and following the reference lists of the scholarly sources (arxiv, semantic
scholar) and related cited papers. Finally, we ended up with large corpus of full-text documents. The next
challenging part is that how we can create the difficult questions as STEM benchmarks from the sources, as
the entire source is not relevant to construct the questions. Therefore, we built a pipeline which considers
the extraction of useful in the content from the sources for generating expert reasoning level question, so
we built a pipeline that first extracts the useful content and then generates questions as shown in Figures
26 and 27.
sections.content: Evidence Extraction. reasoning model reads each document and extracts few short, self-contained evidence passages, such as theorem, derivation, an experimental result, or key definition. Each passage is backed by exact quotes from the source and tagged with key terms that link it to related documents. Question generation uses only these passages, not the full document. Single-hop and multi-hop questions. Questions are generated either from single document (singlehop) or from small group of related documents (multi-hop). multi-hop question must use evidence from every document in its group, so answering it requires connecting ideas across sources rather than recalling single fact. Each generation call follows one question pattern, such as applying theorem to specific case, calculating from formula, or comparing alternatives. If the evidence does not support the pattern, the model returns no question instead of forcing one. Standalone format. The solver sees only the question text. The evidence, answer, and reasoning stay hidden. Along with each question, the model writes step-by-step solution plan in which every step 64 Figure 26: Source-grounded question synthesis pipeline. builds on evidence or on an earlier step. It also explains why the answer cannot be reached by shortcut. Quality checks. Every question goes through automatic checks that confirm it is grounded in the evidence and does not give away its answer. question is rejected if: its solution plan has too few reasoning steps; it relies on too little evidence; it contains steps that the final answer does not depend on; it refers to material the solver cannot see; its answer is copied directly from the evidence. These checks keep questions that need real multi-step reasoning and remove those that could be answered by lookup or shortcuts. Solver rollouts. separate model attempts each accepted question using only the question text. We save its full reasoning trace and final answer as training data. Feedback-driven question synthesis. Apart from the above pipeline, we built second pipeline on the same sources. Instead of building difficulty into the question format, it measures difficulty while questions are being generated and uses that signal to make them harder: Passage grouping. reasoning model extracts passages from each source. The passages are then grouped into small sets drawn from few related documents. Each group gets randomly sampled settings, such as reasoning type, answer format, and question style, to keep the questions varied. Solver feedback loop. The model first writes batch of questions from its group. smaller model then tries to answer each question without any supporting context. The first model is told which questions were solved and asked for new, harder batch. In early tests, simply asking for hard questions had little effect. What helped was naming the questions that had been solved, and asking whether an expert could answer them from general knowledge alone. 65 Figure 27: Feedback-driven question synthesis pipeline. Domain-specific question styles. Each topic is routed to domain family (formal, quantitative, empirical, or interpretive), and the allowed question styles change with the family. This keeps, for example, humanities questions from being forced into artificial calculations. The pipeline also removes low-quality and homework-help sources, and spends more of its budget on fields that existing datasets cover poorly. Difficulty scoring. Each question is answered twice by the smaller model, once with its supporting context and once without. The answers are graded by automatic answer matching rather than by an LLM judge. The most valuable questions are those that can be answered only with the context: they are grounded in the source but cannot be solved from general knowledge. The two pipelines approach difficulty from opposite sides. This pipeline measures difficulty and uses feedback to raise it. The first builds difficulty into the question by requiring multi-step solution over hidden evidence. Our move to standalone questions came from this pipelines finding that questions paired with supporting context were often too easy.

sections.title:
5.12.5 Research lab: a simulated research community
Research is done by communities of researchers who cooperate and compete at the same time. They split
up work, share code, and co-author papers, but they also race for priority, credit, attention, and resources.
Agent trajectories collected on isolated tasks show none of this behavior. To produce data that does, we
built a research lab: a persistent, real-time simulation where a group of researcher agents works toward
new results on a shared pool of open problems (Figure 28). The lab draws its problems from the task
pipelines of this section. Its open problems are Harbor tasks, and its method-improvement tasks are the
autoresearch environments of §5.12.2.
sections.content: The world is built on Concordia (Vezhnevets et al., 2023). game master holds the world state, applies the rules, and checks the win conditions. Each world has ten researchers. Each one is an OpenCode agent (Anomaly, 2026) with persona (name, temperament, and writing register), disciplinary profile such as computational physicist or pure mathematician, and matching bundle of skills and scientific libraries. researcher has private workspace and acts on the shared world only through command-line tool. Every call resolves immediately against the live world, so the world keeps changing while the agent thinks. Long sessions are split into work periods with context compaction, and recall command searches what the agent observed in earlier periods. Kimi K3 (Kimi Team, 2026b) plays every role: the researchers, 66 the game master, the conference referee, and the simulated public. Open problems and the conference. public board lists about 1.5k open problems from numerical analysis, classical analysis, materials science, statistics, and scientific computing, each with hardness rating from 1 to 5. Pulling problem delivers its full statement privately but does not reserve it. submission is folder with paper, the answer, and the code that produced it. An automated conference first checks the answer, then referee judges whether the paper derives it end to end. Thin papers are rejected even when the answer is correct. The first accepted paper closes the problem and later submissions are scooped, so researchers must trade speed against rigor. Autoresearch board. About 870 method-improvement tasks come as git repositories with metric, baseline, and target. Submissions are committed workspaces with report and are evaluated asynchronously on the host. The current best result on each task earns leaderboard point, and its authors may write it up for the conferences Autoresearch track. Credit and the economy. solo paper of value pays w, while paper with two or more authors shares larger pot of 2.2w, so collaboration pays. Researchers start with 100 coins and can pay one another for anything they agree on, such as solving, writing, co-authorship slot, or promotion. market lists offers and requests and holds payment in escrow when the deliverable is file. Public square and coordination. An OASIS social network (Yang et al., 2024) is the only public channel. It is populated by large simulated public of journalists, students, aggregators, and skeptics who react to posts that interest them, and accepted papers and leaderboard verdicts are announced there. In private, researchers coordinate through direct messages, group chats, file sharing, and shared git repositories. Win conditions. The game ends when one researcher reaches target in public engagement, paper credit, autoresearch credit, or coins. These four goals reward different strategies, such as grinding papers, topping leaderboards, building an audience, or trading. Collaborative variant. second configuration removes competition. The team shares one goal, bringing every task on the autoresearch board to its target, and it divides the work by expertise, shares partial results early, and pools its submission budget. Trajectory export. At the end of run we export each researchers full agent trajectory in two views: with compaction turns removed, and split into one segment per work period. The compaction turns themselves form third set. We also keep selected subset of the simulated publics decisions. Every record passes the same filter as our SFT data, which rejects records where the model identifies itself as another model, anonymizes run-specific paths and account names, and computes token statistics. From 2026-08-20 snapshot of 380 runs (238 played to completion), we obtained 3.0k researcher trajectories (338M tokens), 0.4k compaction records (52M tokens), and 31.8k public-account decisions (341M tokens). We use the resulting 35k records (0.73B tokens) in the mid-training stage.

5.12.6 Data-science trajectories from Kaggle competitions
Data analysis is central to scientific work, from interpreting experimental measurements to evaluating
predictive models. Our goal is to improve our models’ performance on data-science tasks by training
on trajectories that cover data inspection, preprocessing, model development, and evaluation. We built
a pipeline (Figure 29) that converts Kaggle competition datasets (Kaggle, n.d.) into MLE-bench-style
tasks (Chan et al., 2024), aligning the public data layout, submission interface, and tool-using agent
workflow with the setting used to evaluate the trained models. We organize these tasks into five workflow
categories, summarized in Table 24.

The solver received training labels and held-out inputs, while the corresponding answers remained private. This provided local evaluation when Kaggles official test labels were unavailable (Chan et al., 2024).
