Solution generation. We used Kimi K3 (Kimi Team, 2026b) and DeepSeek-V4-Flash (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) through OpenCode (Anomaly, 2026), assigning task preparation and solving to separate agent roles with different filesystem permissions. Within bounded search budget, subsequent attempts received the previous score, metric direction, and summaries of earlier approaches to guide alternative strategies. Scores came from our locally prepared tasks; comparisons with Kaggle medal thresholds were approximate and did not constitute official competition results. Repair and monitoring. Failures in the adapter and solver stages were handled by two dedicated repair agents. An adapter-repair agent received task-validation errors and corrected the prepared task, while submission-repair agent received sanitized failure feedback, without private labels, scores, or grader code, and regenerated the submission. Each repair was followed by validation and, for submissions, grading. separate solver-monitor agent inspected execution activity, artifact changes, and recent tool events to identify stalled sessions and inform controller-managed recovery. Trajectory collection. We trained only on solver-agent trajectories, which capture the reasoning involved in solving each task alongside tool calls and execution outputs. We converted these records into training conversations and applied the shared dataprocessing checks for conversation structure, tool-call consistency, reasoning content, repetition, template leakage, and token length. After training, we use MLE-bench to evaluate model checkpoints on its 75 machinelearning engineering competitions. We retain only the solver and submission-repair roles from our synthesis pipeline, since MLE-bench already provides task descriptions, prepared data splits, submission requirements, and task-specific graders. Our harness exposes each competitions prepared/public/ files in the solvers public/ directory, including the task description, training and test data, and submission examples where provided. Private reference answers in prepared/private/ remain inaccessible to the solver. sections.title:
5.12.8 From research proofs to verifiable ML-theory tasks
A growing body of work mines the research literature for mathematical benchmarks and training data (Zhang
et al., 2025b; Dekoninck et al., 2026b). Exact-answer extraction covers results with a single numerical
or closed-form answer (Zhang et al., 2025b), and proof-oriented approaches use LLM judges or formal
proof infrastructure (Peyronnet et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026b). ML-theory results have two characteristic
features: they are mostly bounds and rates whose constants the paper leaves unspecified, and they are
proved through long chains of lemmas. Our ML-theory task generation pipeline is built around both. It
turns a paper’s proof into a self-contained problem set in which every intermediate result is graded, grades
bounds and rates with executable checks, and builds each task through specialized roles that review and
stress-test it before release.
sections.content: The proof tree becomes the problem set. For each paper, the pipeline extracts the proof dependency graph and selects subtree around central result. Boundary results are given as assumptions, and each internal result becomes subproblem that later subproblems may cite. task passes only when every subproblem passes, so the reward measures how well model composes intermediate results, tracks the assumptions they use, and gets their parameter dependence right. Executable checks for bounds and rates. Each subproblem has deterministic checker that relaxes exactly what the source paper leaves free. Closed forms are compared symbolically at random parameter values. Bounds stated with O() constants are compared up to one positive constant, with 70 Figure 30: From technical documents to interactive simulator tasks. design agent defines the task, and an implementation agent writes the simulator. Candidates are checked for correct execution, repeatability, and direct leaks of hidden values. policy using only information available to the solver must then beat both inaction and random actions by preset margin in average score across the same test seeds. Eligible failures receive bounded repair and are checked again. Accepted tasks support trajectory generation and automatic scoring. the dependence on every parameter checked exactly. Rates are checked through their values across scales, and constant certificates are checked as systems of inequalities. Reference answers come from executing reference solution, which must pass every checker. Specialized roles that guard task quality. Each role in the pipeline is responsible for one aspect of task quality, and every construction step pairs proposer with reviewer. The extractors proof graph is checked against the paper, the task writers subproblems are checked by critic for well-posedness, and the reformulators rewrite is checked by its own reviewer. The reformulator targets the crux of the central result: it rewrites the root question so that the graded quantity follows from the key step of the argument, for example an instance-specific constant or jointly optimized parameter, which model reaches by carrying out that step. Each finished task then goes through three independent quality checks. cold solver tests self-containment: it attempts the task from its text alone and reports any missing assumption or ambiguous reading, which is repaired by adding the missing statement or pinning the intended reading. shortcut probe tests that the reward requires the derivation: it tries to pass the real checker with an answer produced by guessing or by reusing given, and task whose checker accepts such an answer is tightened or rejected. consistency check tests fidelity to the source by comparing the reference answers with the papers theorem. Source papers come from ten arXiv primary categories (math.OC, stat.ML, cs.LG, cs.IT, math.PR, math.NA, cs.DS, eess.SY, math.ST, cs.DM), covering high-dimensional statistics, robust learning, generalization, online learning and bandits, optimization, concentration, differential privacy, control, numerical analysis, information theory, and deep learning theory. We measure difficulty with an open-weight solver agent, MiniMax-M3, run four times per task; solve rates span the full range from 0/4 to 4/4. All tasks run in Harbor environments with deterministic, code-only scoring. The agent roles of the pipeline are run with Kimi K3, and we record its trajectories: pipeline-building trajectories, which show how tasks are constructed from source papers, and solver trajectories on the resulting tasks. Figure 31 gives an overview. 71 Figure 31: ML-Theory Task Generation Pipeline. (1) subtree around central result is selected from the papers proof graph; boundary results become assumptions and internal results become subtasks. (2) Proposerreviewer pairs write the subtasks and harden the central question. (3) An executed reference solution and checker per subtask decide the answers; three quality checks (cold solve, shortcut probe, consistency check) send the task back for revision or reject it. (4) In Harbor, solver is rewarded only if every checker passes. Violet: agent roles; teal: executed code.

sections.title:
5.13 Long Context Document Understanding
To strengthen the model’s ability to read and reason over documents, in particular long ones, we synthesize
two data subsets with two pipelines. The first, LCQA, generates question–answer pairs over single long
documents:
long documents are first annotated and filtered down to high-quality passages, questions
are then written from those passages and trained with the full document in context, covering retrieval,
comparison, causal and multi-hop task types. The second, LCR, targets multi-document reasoning, where
the answer only exists once evidence from several long documents is combined. Both subsets carry the
reasoning trace of the answering model and are emitted as two-turn conversations.
sections.content: Long-context question answering (LCQA). LCQA is built around single constraint we call answer invariance: question is written about short, high-quality passage, but the training example presents the entire document that passage came from. Because the answer is fully determined by the passage, it remains correct when the context expands, but reaching it requires searching tens of thousands of tokens rather than reading short one. This avoids the two common failure modes of synthetic long-context data, namely padding short QA pair with filler (a needle that was never hidden) and prompting over whole document (which tends to produce questions about its opening pages). The pipeline17 has two stages: long-document annotation, and question and answer synthesis from the annotated passages. Stage 1: long-document annotation. The input is every document between 8k and 512k tokens in our pre-training corpus, spanning web, scientific, code and math, book and encyclopedic sources. document of this length is rarely uniformly good or uniformly poor, so scoring it as one unit discards exactly the information we need, which is where its good parts are. The standard quality scorers also transfer poorly to documents of this length: the transformer-based FineWeb-Edu (Lozhkov et al., 2024) regressor truncates its input, so whole-document score for 128k-token document is in practice score for its first few hundred tokens, and the fastText classifiers are trained on web pages that are far shorter than anything in this corpus, so their bag-of-n-gram statistics are diluted at these lengths. Both arguments point the same 17https://github.com/ifm-ai/LCQA

sections.content: 57.97M 3.59M 0.38M 61.94M 8.8% 34.9% 40.4% 784.1B 205.7B 60.1B 10.5% 1,049.9B 13.7% 39.4% 38.0% 20.1% Table 25: LCQA long-document annotation yield by document length. way, and we therefore make the section, rather than the document, the unit of judgment: 1. Structure-aware splitting. Each document is cut into sections of at most 512 tokens by splitter chosen per source: semantic splitter for prose, Markdown splitter for papers and books, and tree-sitter splitter for code and math18. Splitting on structure rather than at fixed stride keeps headings with their bodies and code blocks intact, so that section is self-contained passage able to host question on its own, and it keeps every section within the input budget of the scorers that judge it. 2. Section scoring. Every section receives three quality judgments, from DCLM/ELI5 (Li et al., 2024), PreSelect (Shum et al., 2025) and the FineWeb-Edu educational-value regressor (Lozhkov et al., 2024), plus multi-dimensional toxicity score19. 3. Rank bucketing. The three quality scores live on incomparable scales (two probabilities and 05 regression), so each is mapped onto shared 019 scale using cut points from the corpus score distribution. 4. Document filtering. Section scores are aggregated to the document and the document is dropped unless its means clear every threshold (FineWeb-Edu bucket 17, ELI5 and PreSelect 10, toxicity 0.2, length 16k tokens). 5. Passage sampling. Within each surviving document, only sections that independently clear stricter bar are eligible; we sample four and pair each with the full document text. Table 25 reports the yield. From 61.9M documents and 1.05T tokens we retain 6.5M documents (10.5% of documents, 20.1% of tokens) and emit roughly 26M passagedocument pairs. Notably, the keep rate rises steeply with document length, from 8.8% in the 8k32k range to 40.4% in the 128k512k range: text that sustains itself over 128k tokens is typically book, review article or textbook, so length acts as quality signal rather than liability. Stage 2: question and answer synthesis. For each surviving document, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B (Qwen Team, 2026) sees only its sampled passages, in document order, and writes one question about them. Answer invariance decides which questions may be asked: the answer must be fully determined by the passages, so the prompt rules out questions whose answer can change when the context grows, such as counts, lists of all items, or questions about the documents structure. Within this constraint, three knobs are drawn per document: Task type (17): retrieving stated fact or an attribute of an entity; relationships and comparisons; multi-hop questions that combine passages or resolve an indirect reference; causal, consequence, 18We use the semantic-text-splitter library, with token counts from tiktoken. Sources with reliable markup (arXiv, PubMed Central, PG19, MegaMath) are handed to the splitter whole; for the rest, we first segment on sentence boundaries and call the splitter only on pieces that are still over budget. 19From the detoxify library (multilingual model), https://github.com/unitaryai/detoxify. 73 purpose and conditional reasoning; methods and processes; the state of an entity or value at specific point in the text; definitions, examples, inference from stated facts, and stated opinions. Question format (9): open-ended, short answer, yes/no, multiple choice, true/false, fill-in-the-blank, comparative, temporal, and extractive (asking for the exact phrase the text uses). Some task types allow only the formats that suit them. Difficulty (3): easy (answer stated in similar wording), medium (connecting two or three pieces of information, some paraphrasing) or hard (synthesis, different wording, multi-step reasoning), drawn with weights 0.1/0.4/0.5. The question is returned as JSON and validated against its format. The same model then answers it from the passages alone, and only the training conversation replaces the passages with the full document (5.16). The question is placed before or after the document in one of 48 layouts that vary its prefix and the framing of the document. Of 6.5M documents, 99.6% yield training conversation: 6.48M conversations and 211B tokens, of which 5.05M are 8k32k tokens long, 1.31M 32k128k and 0.12M 128k512k. Long-context reasoning (LCR). The LCR subset targets questions that can only be answered by combining evidence scattered across several long documents. The documents are real web documents from domains such as company filings and earnings materials, government consultation responses, industry reports, legal documents and academic papers, and set is built so that its documents are tied together by shared axis: the same company across successive reporting periods, peer companies in the same period, one event covered by different document kinds, many respondents to one consultation, or several reports on one theme. Typical questions rank peer companies by figure each reports separately, compute change across companys quarterly filings, count how many consultation respondents took given position, or list the entities that satisfy condition across collection of reports. Its design is inspired by the AA-LCR benchmark (Artificial Analysis Team, 2025). Each sample is set of 324 documents totaling roughly 70k384k tokens, question whose answer must be derived across documents rather than looked up in one, short verifiable answer, and the full reasoning trace of the answering model. Pipeline. The pipeline runs in seven stages: documents are retrieved and packed into coherent sets, evidence passages are selected programmatically, question is generated over them, it is answered from the full set, its difficulty is labeled, the sample is verified for multi-document necessity and correctness, and the result is post-processed into training conversation. 1. Retrieval and assembly. For each target set, we enumerate retrieval plan from an entity registry, period grid and the document kinds appropriate to the domain, holding the shared axis fixed and varying the rest, and issue the resulting queries to the Keenable20 search and fetch API, restricted to authoritative sites such as regulatory filing databases, consultation portals and preprint servers. Fetched pages are stripped of boilerplate, quality-filtered, checked for relevance to the plan (the target entity must be the subject of the document, not passing mention), deduplicated exactly and by MinHash (Broder, 1997; Lee et al., 2022), and packed to sampled token target. 2. Programmatic grounding. Before the generator sees set, code selects one paragraph from each of three or more distinct documents, scoring for reasoning affordances (numeric density, period markers, definitional language) rather than salience, and preferring passages that share an entity or period. Cross-document necessity and non-salient evidence therefore hold by construction, at zero model cost. 3. Question generation. large reasoning model sees the grounding passages and the whole set and 20https://keenable.ai/ 74 writes question that needs every passage, prefers derivation over lookup, and has short atomic answer. Mechanical guards reject over-long questions and the ones that restate the passages figures, with one retry that feeds the violation back. 4. Answering. The answerer sees only documents plus question, in one of 2,880 prompt formats composed from five independent axes (document wrapper, envelope, question position, question delimiter, instruction phrasing), so the model learns the skill rather than scaffold. Half the samples in the 105384k band use our default chat template. The reasoning channel is kept verbatim and never truncated. 5. Difficulty label. deliberately weak long-context model answers the question blind, and whether it succeeds is recorded for every sample. This follows the logic of adversarial filtering (Zellers et al., 2018; Bras et al., 2020), where weaker models success marks an example as easy, except that we keep the label rather than discard the sample. 6. Verification. necessity ablation re-answers the question from each required document alone under the identical template; any match rejects the sample as single-document answerable. This is the document-level form of the disconnected reasoning check used for multi-hop QA datasets (Min et al., 2019; Trivedi et al., 2020), where questions meant to need two passages turned out to be answerable from one. Survivors are then judged for correctness, ambiguity and format by an LLM judge (Zheng et al., 2023) from different model family than the answerer (enforced in code), or, on the deadline-bound runs, by agreement between the answerer and the question generator. Every row records which chain verified it. 7. Post-processing. The prompt is rebuilt from the document store and hash-verified against what the answerer actually saw, then emitted as two-turn conversation with separate think and content fields, stamped with run, verification chain and sample id. Three production runs over two document stores (one for 70128k prompts, one for 105384k) produced 47,653 verified conversations totaling 6.2B tokens after the shared quality gate, with prompts from 63k to 391k tokens, answers averaging about 10 tokens and reasoning traces averaging about 3k. further 145k conversations that failed verification are kept as separately labeled tier. Accepted samples cover all seven domains and all five assembly patterns, with company filings the largest share.

sections.title:
5.14 Abstention
The abstention data consists of factoid questions generated from public sources across a diverse set of
domains and topics, with the goal of training models to learn when to abstain. Questions that are
unambiguous and can be reliably answered from public information retain their reference answers, while
questions that cannot be reliably answered are assigned [IDK]. The data is constructed using a three-stage
pipeline. Passage Collection gathers text from openly licensed public sources across domains. Grounded
QA Generation converts these passages into standalone factoid question–answer pairs whose answers are
verified against the source passages. The Abstention Review then identifies questions that depend on
source/temporal-specific information and relabels their targets as [IDK].
sections.content: Passage Collection. The first stage collects passages from public online sources across different domains, with predefined target number of passages for each domain. Each domain is associated with set of sources and retrieval parameters, such as search terms, API endpoints, or regulation titles. Records are retrieved through public APIs or publicly accessible web pages and converted into self-contained text passages using source-specific preprocessing. Structured records are rendered into readable text, web pages are cleaned and segmented at sentence boundaries, and regulation sections are preserved as complete 75 Figure 32: Factoid & Source-Specific Question Generation Pipeline. Well-posed factoid questions drive factual recall capability, while ambiguous source-specific questions drive abstention capability. passages. The resulting passages are normalized and filtered to remove short or duplicate content, including duplicates identified through source-specific record identifiers. Each retained passage is assigned stable identifier and preserves its source URL, license information, and snapshot date, allowing this provenance to be carried through to the QA pairs generated from it. Grounded QA Generation. The second stage converts each collected passage into factoid questionanswer pairs that are realistic and grounded in the source passage. An LLM generates six candidate pairs from each passage, each with short answer and supporting quote. LLM-based filters assess the formulation of each question, rejecting those that depend on implicit context, reveal the answer, are malformed, or refer to the source through phrases such as the passage, the source, or according to. Candidates that fail are rewritten using the filter feedback and evaluated again, with up to two rewrite attempts. Rule-based filters further enforce basic requirements on the question and answer and verify that the answer or its supporting evidence appears in the passage. grounding check then confirms against the passage that the answer is correct and supported by the cited evidence. Finally, each question is compared with previously accepted questions to remove exact or highly similar duplicates. Abstention Review. The final stage determines whether each accepted question should retain its reference answer or be assigned an abstention target. Although the previous stage ensures that each question is well posed and grounded in its source passage, some answers remain specific to particular record, product, version, jurisdiction, or point in time. An LLM therefore reviews each question together with its answer, supporting evidence, and source metadata, and decides whether to retain the reference answer or assign [IDK]. Questions are marked for abstention when their answers depend on source-specific information, such as product calories or product recall, or on time-sensitive information such as current statistics, policies, statuses, or regulatory records without clear date or version. In contrast, general facts and clearly dated historical facts retain their reference answers. Abstained questions remain in the dataset, but their labels are replaced with [IDK], while the original answers and review results are preserved as metadata. Trajectory Generation & Selection. Using these synthesized questions, we generate four trajectories per question using the abstention prompt from AA-Omniscience (Jackson et al., 2025), which allows the model to either provide an answer or abstain when additional information is needed. We retain trajectories that 76 produce either fully correct answer or an abstention, while discarding incorrect and partially correct responses. Sampling multiple trajectories captures differences in the models response to the same question. In particular, model may answer question correctly in some trajectories while abstaining in others when it determines that additional context is required. As such, retaining both types of valid trajectories provides training examples for learning when to answer confidently and when to abstain.

sections.title:
5.15 Browser Use
The browser-use pipeline synthesizes realistic tasks on live, public websites, which a browser agent then
executes to produce multi-turn trajectories.
It faces two main challenges. The first is feasibility: a
website is an environment we can only observe, so a task is useful only if the site supports it at rollout
time. The second is diversity: left unconstrained, a generator drifts toward short look-up questions and
underrepresents the transactional, multi-constraint, and underspecified requests that real users make. The
pipeline has three stages: URL collection, page acquisition, and reverse task synthesis, which is controlled
by three axes (intent, difficulty, and ambiguity).
sections.content: Website collection. We begin with 84 unique seed websites from Mind2Web (Deng et al., 2023) and WebVoyager (He et al., 2024), utilizing only the domain information rather than benchmark instructions. This set is expanded to 544 candidate URLs through human-assisted LLM augmentation. To ensure accessibility and relevance, we visit each candidate using headless Chromium via Playwright. We discard URLs that time out or return HTTP status codes of 400 or higher. For successful requests, we retain the final URL after any redirects, as regional redirects can alter the content visible to the agent. Finally, we download the rendered homepage, which serves as the sole input for the task generator. Reverse task synthesis. An LLM reads the homepage snapshot and writes tasks that start from an entry point visible on the page and refer only to content the page evidences. We sample three axes outside the model: intent (info-seeking, transactional, tool-use, messaging, or navigation), difficulty (D0 to D3, from at most one constraint to six or more), and ambiguity (A0 to A3, from single correct answer to vague goal that requires clarification). For each page, we draw (difficulty, ambiguity) pairs without replacement from the 16 combinations, and for each pair the model writes five tasks, one per intent, which keeps the distribution from collapsing onto look-up queries. Bundles that fail schema or label checks are rejected. We run Kimi K2.5 (Kimi Team, 2026a) in the browser-use agent harness (Müller and Žunič, 2024) on the synthesized tasks against live websites, and keep trajectories where the models self-evals succeed. We use the resulting 45k trajectories (1.5 tokens) in the mid-training stage. (cid:17) Derive tasks from what the page offers, not from what the model imagines Prompting model to generate browser tasks from only website name or seed instruction yields fluent but often infeasible tasks. Such tasks may require filters, tools, or pages that the site does not provide, or refer to content that no longer exists. Since the open web is outside our control, post-generation feasibility checks are costly and unreliable. We instead reverse the synthesis order: we observe the live page first and write tasks only against the affordances it exposes. In this way, feasibility is guaranteed by construction, not by post-hoc filter.

sections.title:
5.16 Beyond Teacher Imitation
Rolling out a teacher on a task and recording what it does yields trajectories that are at best as good as the
teacher. They are limited by the teacher’s context window, its attention over long inputs, its own decisions
about when to stop, and its failures on the hardest tasks. Our post-training data generation methods
sections.content: 77 instead produce training trajectories that the teacher could not generate on its own. The common idea is to separate what the teacher sees during generation from what we record for training. In long-context question answering, the teacher works with few focused passages, and the full document is added only to the training trajectory (5.16.1). Length-controlled generation keeps the teachers working context short while the recorded conversation grows to target of up to 512k tokens (5.16.2). Multi-turn PR chains run each PR of repository in fresh session and join the sessions into one long coding session (5.16.3). privileged advisor checks the solvers work against the reference solution and hidden tests, and inserts cues into its reasoning when it is about to submit flawed solution, without revealing the answer (5.16.4). Finally, augmentation techniques vary the system prompts, answer formats, and tool interfaces of each task, so that the model does not depend on single presentation (5.16.5).

sections.title:
5.16.2 Length-controlled generation
Long agentic trajectories are hard to obtain from a teacher for two reasons. The teacher’s context is
bounded, so a 512k-token research conversation cannot be generated in one pass, and quality degrades
well before the limit (Liu et al., 2024). The teacher also decides on its own when to stop, and given an
open-ended question, it tends to answer after a handful of searches, however much there is to find. For
the search conversations (§5.10) we therefore separate what the teacher sees from what we record, and we
make the length of the trajectory a parameter of generation.
sections.content: Working context and trace. The generator keeps two views of the conversation. The trace records every message and tool result and grows up to the target length. The working context, which is what the teacher receives at each step, pins the system prompt and the first user message and keeps only the most recent messages, at most 100 messages and 100k tokens. Documents are truncated to 30k characters when read, so that single document cannot fill the window. After each burst of tool calls, the teacher writes short summary of what it found, and these summaries carry the findings forward in compact form as older tool results leave the window. Every assistant turn is written from the beginning of the trace and recent suffix of it, so it never refers to content that the trace does not contain, while the teacher never holds more than 100k tokens. Pacing to target. Each query is assigned target of 32k, 128k, or 512k tokens. Research continues until the trace reaches 80% of its target or 100 turns, and the remaining budget goes to final synthesis, written without tool access from the working context. Between research steps, the simulated user samples its next message type (react to finding, drill deeper, redirect, challenge, clarify, or build upon) with weights that depend on what just happened. While the trace length is below 60% of its target, message types that invite wrap-up are removed. When the teacher stalls, the generator injects short request to continue. These requests are runtime scaffolding rather than user input, so we remove them from the saved trace. 78 Figure 33: How one PR chain becomes single long episode. Each PR is attempted in its own fresh agent session against the same working tree, so state reaches the next turn two ways: through the filesystem, which accumulates, and through compacted handoff, which does not. Per-turn context therefore stays roughly constant however long the episode runs, while cumulative token usage climbs until it crosses the budget, at which point the run stops and the partial episode is kept. The whole episode runs inside sandbox in which the network tools are gated: dependency installs resolve against local package mirror and git operations against local repository mirror, so build can still fetch what it needs while the obvious routes to the upstream change are closed. The gating is at the tool layer rather than the network layer, so the public internet remains reachable by an agent that writes its own client; we did not observe this in the trajectories we inspected. The number of turns an episode reaches is set by the budget rather than by the number of PRs the chain offers. The resulting traces land close to their target lengths: median traces reach 95%, 87%, and 82% of the 32k, 128k, and 512k targets, respectively, and 94%, 97%, and 81% of traces fall within 25% of their target.

sections.title:
5.16.3 Multi-turn PR chains
The PR rollouts of §5.5 are single-turn, but real coding sessions are longer. A developer asks for one feature
after another in the same repository, and each change builds on the earlier ones. We create trajectories
with many user turns by chaining the PRs of a repository in their original order and giving them to an
agent one at a time in a single checkout, so that each PR becomes a new user turn. After each turn, the
agent’s work is summarized into a short handoff for the next turn and, at the end, the turns are joined into
one multi-turn trajectory (Figure 33).
sections.content: Chain construction. chain should look like the history of real project in which one codebase changes step by step. We therefore group the PRs by repository and order them by PR number, which follows the order in which they were opened. chain starts with the lowest-numbered PR which becomes the first user turn. Every later turn also gets task written from its PR, which states the goal without giving away the patch. This yields 10,175 chains, one per repository, covering 2M PRs. The median chain has 113 PRs, the 90th percentile 361, and the longest 33,766, while the shortest has two. record holds at most 50 PRs, so the 7,761 chains that are longer continue in further records, each starting with the next PR of its chain. Sandbox. Each chain runs in its own sandbox checkout at the base commit of the chains first PR for the repository. We remove the origin remote and the reflog, so the checkout holds the base state and nothing after it. The change that each turn asks for already exists upstream, and fetching it would be the 79 cheapest way to appear to succeed. The sandbox therefore blocks curl, wget, web search, and page fetches, as well as git clone, fetch, pull, and ls-remote in every spelling we could list. Builds still need their dependencies, so pip, npm, Go, Maven, apt, and other package managers point to local Nexus mirror, and GitHub URLs are rewritten to local Gitea mirror. The blocking happens at the tool level, not the network level. An agent could still reach the internet by writing its own client, although we did not see this in the trajectories we inspected. Chain rollouts. Each user turn should start where the previous one ended, as in real coding session, but the agents context should not grow with every PR. We run DeepSeek-V4-Flash (0731) (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) with thinking in the OpenCode agent harness (Anomaly, 2026) and start fresh agent session for each PR on the same working tree, so the code carries over between turns while the context does not. turn therefore starts from the agents own work on the earlier PRs, not from the upstream history that its PR was written against. What the session knows about the earlier turns comes from the handoff described below. turn that stops before the agent finishes the task is resumed in the same session up to three times, and is otherwise kept as it is. Runs are bounded by cumulative token budget of 512k rather than by the number of PRs. The budget is checked before each turn starts, so the last turn may go over it, and run that stops at the budget counts as complete. The runs have between 3 and 27 turns, since run can spend the whole budget on three PRs in large codebase or work through twenty-seven in small one. Context handoff. fresh session knows nothing about the earlier turns, and passing it their full history would make the context grow with every PR. Instead, after each turn, the same model summarizes it in separate call. The input is the previous handoff, the last 4,000 characters of the agents final message, the PR and the task title of the turn that just ended, and the task for the next turn. The model returns JSON object with nine fields: completed work, current state, evidence and uncertainty (split into facts backed by evidence and points that still need checking), work in progress, constraints, critical context, verification history, relevant files and symbols, and known risks. The handoff is placed at the start of the next turns prompt. Since each handoff is written from the previous one and not from the full history, its size stays about the same however many turns have run. Multi-turn trajectories. For training, we want the model to see the whole session, not summary of it. We therefore drop the handoffs and join the sessions of run into one conversation. Each PRs task becomes user turn, followed by everything the agent did for that PR, so one trajectory contains many user turns on codebase that changes from turn to turn. If joined conversation is longer than 512k tokens, we drop user turns from the end until it fits, keeping at least two. The resulting trajectories contain about 7B tokens.

sections.title:
5.16.4 Advisor-guided trajectory generation
Agentic coding rollouts often fail not because the solver makes no progress, but because it terminates at
the wrong point. A solver may repair the most visible symptom while leaving a secondary requirement
unresolved, submit after narrow validation, or continue editing after reaching a correct solution and
subsequently undo it. We address these failures with a privileged advisor: a rollout-time controller that can
inspect reference material unavailable to the solver, but cannot edit the repository or act on the task itself.
Its sole role is to decide whether the solver’s next action should be accepted or regenerated. Figure 34
illustrates one review step, and our implementation is publicly available (Pimpalkhute et al., 2026).21
sections.content: Privileged review. Let πθ denote the solver policy with parameters θ, the public task specification, the privileged task material, and ht the public solver history at turn t, i.e., all previously committed solver 21https://github.com/ifm-ai/advisor 80 Figure 34: Privileged advisor intervention during rollout generation. At designated checkpoints, the advisor consults private evidence and either accepts the draft or returns privilege-free cue for solver revision. Only the selected solver response is committed; privileged material never enters the trajectory or solver sandbox. responses together with their tool and terminal observations. At each turn, the solver first samples provisional (draft) response yt. Let Finish(yt) be the indicator that the draft invokes the finish tool, the periodic review interval, the per-attempt intervention budget, and nt the number of interventions already used in the current attempt. The advisor reviews every proposed finish action and, when periodic review is enabled, every k-th solver turn. Generation and the review gate gt {0, 1} are yt πθ( x, ht), gt = 1{nt < B} 1{Finish(yt) (t mod = 0)} . The periodic term is omitted when periodic review is disabled. When gt = 1, the draft is passed to the advisor Aϕ, separate language model with parameters ϕ. The advisor receives the public specification x, bounded rendering of ht, the draft yt, and the privileged material z, which contains the reference solution, hidden verifier tests, and private task notes. Because the advisor is stateful within an attempt (see below), it also receives pt1, the private plan it produced at its most recent review (empty at the first review), and H<t, the set of solver-facing hints it issued at earlier reviews in the same attempt. The advisor then produces decision dt = Aϕ (cid:0)x, z, ht, yt, pt1, H<t (cid:1), dt = (cid:0)ft, rt, at, pt, ηt, δt (cid:1), where ft {0, 1} is an intervention flag, rt reason code, at discrete action, pt the updated private plan (carried forward as the next reviews pt1), ηt solver-safe hint (added to the hint history H), and δt private diagnosis. The action set contains CONTINUE (accept the draft), CONFIRM_AND_SUBMIT (confirm correct implementation), and corrective actions that ask the solver to re-check requirements, trace state transitions, validate more broadly, or reconsider its submission. Each decision is strictly validated against this schema; malformed decisions are retried rather than interpreted heuristically. The advisor is instructed to assess functional correctness rather than similarity to the reference patch. In particular, it checks requirement coverage, interacting state transitions, and whether the solver has produced sufficient execution evidence to justify submission. Selective intervention. Let I(dt) denote the solver-facing cue compiled from the advisor decision, and let ˆyt denote the revised response that the solver regenerates after receiving this cue. The response committed 81 to the trajectory is yt = yt, ˆyt, gt = 0 or at = CONTINUE, ˆyt πθ( x, ht, I(dt)), otherwise. For models supporting reasoning continuation, I(dt) is built from the hint ηt and inserted as the opening of the solvers next reasoning block. It is written in the solvers first-person register and ends on an unresolved evidentiary gap, leaving the solver to derive the next command and the correction itself. For other models, the action at is mapped to fixed, task-agnostic self-check instruction. When additional work is required, the finish tool is removed from the revision call, forcing the solver to take substantive action before submitting again. The complementary CONFIRM_AND_SUBMIT action retains the finish tool when periodic review finds that the repository is already correct and further editing is more likely to be harmful than useful. The advisor is stateful within an attempt. Its private plan pt tracks unresolved requirements across reviews, while the hint history H<t prevents repeated interventions from merely restating arguments already visible in the solvers replayed reasoning. If the same gap persists, the advisor must identify new angle grounded in public evidence, such as an unexecuted trace or contradiction in the solvers observations, without disclosing the missing implementation. Figure 35: Fraction of tasks solved without and with the advisor, by category. Advised reruns are applied only to tasks the solver failed on its own. Privileged-information isolation. The private context is loaded only on the rollout host and is never placed in the solver sandbox. The advisors diagnosis δt and plan pt remain private. Every factual claim in the solver-facing cue I(dt) must be supported by the public task, repository, or terminal evidence already contained in (x, ht, yt). Thus, the advisor may use hidden evidence to identify where the current trajectory is weak, but may not quote or paraphrase hidden tests, reveal expected outputs, or provide the solution. Only the selected solver response is appended, ht+1 = ht yt; the rejected draft, private review, and advisor diagnosis never appear as separate trajectory turns. Advised and ordinary rollouts therefore share the same external representation. Advisor and revision requests use bounded retries and 82 fail open to yt when configured to do so. Final correctness is determined exclusively by the benchmark verifier. We additionally audit the resulting trajectories using deterministic leakage checks and separate public-coherence and privileged-leakage judges. The advisor consequently provides privileged process supervision without replacing the solvers own reasoning or execution. Effect on solvable tasks. We ran the solver on 168,990 tasks in five categories (PRism RL tasks, RecursiveTask-Synthesis (RTS) terminal tasks (Li et al., 2026d), other terminal tasks, SWE, and STEM; Table 26) and reran every task it failed to solve with the advisor enabled. Figure 35 reports the outcome. On its own, the solver solved 91,466 tasks (54.1%); advised reruns solved further 31,954, raising the total to 123,420 (73.0%), an increase of 18.9 percentage points. The gain is largest where the unadvised solver is weakest: on RTS, coverage rises from 30.5% to 66.9%. Conversely, STEM, where the solver already succeeds on 87.4% of tasks, gains only 2.7 points. Note that these numbers measure how many tasks yield at least one successful trajectory, which is the quantity that matters for data generation, rather than per-attempt pass rate under matched conditions.

sections.title:
5.16.5 Augmentation techniques
For single turn reasoning tasks, we do prompt augmentation to train the model on tasks with different user
instructions and/or answer format. In particular, we construct a combination of {30 system prompts} ×
{3 answer format}. The system prompt variations cover instructions for different reasoning levels (“reason
step by step”, “reason step by step and never give up” etc.), structured and unstructured reasoning as well
as instructions about self-verification and reflection. The answer format variations include prompting the
model to select one of multiple choices, output short free-form answers (e.g., mathematical expressions for
math/physics reasoning tasks) as well as generating structured outputs in Python, Markdown or JSON
format.
sections.content: For both search and general tool-use data, we augment the corpus by randomizing the tool call interface. For every task, we randomize the names of the tools, the names and order of their parameters, their natural-language descriptions, the way tool results are rendered back to the model, the wording and layout of the instruction, the system prompt, and the convention by which the final answer is submitted: in some trajectories the model commits through dedicated submission tool, while in others no such tool is exposed and the answer must be written as text in prescribed format. For each task, we generate multiple trajectories with different randomized tool call schemas. This method teaches the model to read the tool schema given in each trajectory and act on it, rather than to rely on memorized call signature, and it should make the model less sensitive to the system prompt and tool output formats.

sections.title:
5.17 Programmatic quality and format controls
For K2-V2 (K2 Team, Institute of Foundation Models, 2025), we implemented process_entry, a function
that checks if a training example follows our conversation format. At that time, our SFT data was mostly
non-agentic with little tool use, so checking the format of a conversation was simple. For K2-Horizon, our
focus shifted to agentic behavior in both mid- and post-training, and the data changed accordingly: long
multi-turn trajectories with tool calls, generated by our own pipelines or taken from public datasets. Our
mid-training sources alone contain 13.8M examples with tools and 747K unique tool definitions. In our
earlier training runs, we did few checks on this data and later discovered that it had many issues: tools
that were used but never declared, tool names in the rollout that did not match the declared ones, and
schemas that misled the model about which arguments are allowed. As a result, our initial mid-training
runs produced a model that often hallucinated tool calls. We also found that, at scale, the open models we
use for generation can fall into doom loops, repeating the same action over and over, and that problems in
the environment can lead the model to spend the rollout trying to fix the environment instead of solving
the task. Over time, we collected examples of malformed or corrupted rollouts and added more and more
sections.content: 83 checks. Today, every conversational example in our midand post-training data has to pass process_entry. We release it, together with its tests and the tokenizer and chat template used in training. Design. process_entry takes one example and returns the processed example with its token count, list of reasons for rejection, and record of the changes it made; the example is rejected if and only if the list of reasons is non-empty. Changes are limited to normalizations that do not alter the meaning of the example, such as moving top-level tool list into the system message, unwrapping tools written in the OpenAI function format, parsing tool-call arguments stored as JSON strings, or trimming whitespace in reasoning. The visible replies are never changed, since some tasks depend on exact spacing. All quality checks only reject and never repair, because silently fixing an example would hide broken generator from the person who owns the source. Checks are strict by default, and few settings are chosen per source, such as whether reasoning is required and at which reasoning level. Rules are changed only with explicit manual approval, after measuring the new rule on the full corpus and reading samples of what it rejects. Format and tools. The conversation must follow valid order of system, user, assistant, and tool turns: for example, every tool call must be followed by tool response and every tool response must answer tool call. If the conversation uses tools, all of them must be declared in the system message with name and JSON schema of their parameters, and every tool call is validated against the schema: the tool must exist, required arguments must be present, undeclared arguments are rejected unless the schema explicitly allows them, and argument types and allowed values must match. Agentic data should also teach the model to recover from its own mistakes, so for some sources we enable recovery mode that tolerates an invalid tool call if the environment returned an error, the model did not simply repeat the same failing call, there were at most three errors in row, and the last turn with tool calls succeeded. When reasoning is required, at least one assistant turn must contain it. Reasoning is stored under the field of the requested reasoning effort, and an example without any reasoning is tagged as low effort. Finally, the example is rendered with our chat template in the format used in training, so that problems do not first appear during training, and its token count is saved. Degenerate behavior. We reject examples where the assistant has fallen into loop: the same sentence repeated many times in its reasoning, the same reasoning block repeated across turns, or the same tool call with identical arguments issued again and again. Some loops are only visible through the environment. For example, an agent whose terminal hung kept emitting the same no-op action for hundreds of turns while writing fresh reasoning on every turn, so no check of individual turns could see it. We catch such cases by checking whether the observation that the agent responds to ever changes, which separates stuck agent from legitimate polling, such as waiting for long test run to finish. These checks only look at assistant turns, since user pasting repetitive log or tool returning identical rows is not defect of the training target. They also never penalize length: long reasoning is fine as long as it keeps making progress. Leakage from generation. Generated data carries traces of how it was produced. We reject examples containing special tokens of our chat template, as well as markers of other chat templates and tool-call formats, such as GPT-OSS harmony tokens or the tool-call markup of DeepSeek and Kimi models. Markers are matched by shape rather than as exact strings, because models and converters produce variants with inserted spaces, doubled delimiters, or HTML escaping. For the same reason, we reject examples whose upstream converter records that it modified the data, so that person reviews the converter. subtler leak is the model referring to instructions that the example does not contain. In generations from Kimi K3 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, the model often mentions desired oververbosity level (for example, Desired oververbosity 5), although no such instruction appears anywhere in the example; in one snapshot of our 84 Source Num. Training on such examples would teach our model to react to instructions its user never gave, so we reject assistant turns that refer to an instruction that appears nowhere else in the example. Finally, we check model identity: many of the models we use for generation call themselves Claude or ChatGPT in their reasoning, and system prompts in some public datasets name the model that generated the data. Only assistant and system turns are scanned, so user asking about another model is not rejected. Regression corpus. Most rules started from real example that slipped through the existing checks. We keep such examples, together with hard negatives that look suspicious but are legitimate, in regression corpus. After every change, we verify that each bad example is still caught by at least one rule and that none of the hard negatives is rejected. The released code includes test suite with cases derived from these examples. (cid:17) ALOHOMORA We rely heavily on coding agents for data processing, and when most of dataset is rejected, the easiest fix for an agent is to loosen the validator. So the first lines of process_entry tell coding agents that its rules are load-bearing and may only be changed if the user types secret word: ALOHOMORA. (cid:17) The stuck terminal One trajectory that passed all our checks repeated the same 111-character no-op action 819 times over 1,241 turns, while writing fresh reasoning on every turn, so every check of individual turns looked clean. What finally caught it was looking at the environment rather than the action: the agents observation never changed.

sections.title:
5.18 Public Data Collection
Public SFT datasets for reasoning, tool use, and agent tasks are stored in many different formats. One
dataset may describe its tools in its own way, a second may keep the model’s reasoning in a separate field,
and a third may save agent runs as raw logs instead of conversations. Writing a converter by hand for
each dataset takes too long, and a single general converter rejects most of them. We therefore built a data
processing skill: a written set of steps and rules that a coding agent follows to bring a new dataset into our
sections.content: 85 SFT format. The agent finds out why dataset fails, writes small fix for that dataset, and checks the result. The agent never decides on its own which examples are kept. Every example must pass the same shared validator, process_entry, described in 5.17. Our processing pipeline is summarized in Figure 36. Loading the source. We record the exact dataset, configuration, split, and version for each source, and keep track of where each row came from. For sources saved as logs, we also decide what counts as one training example, because one agent run may be saved many times as it progresses. First test and deciding whether fix is needed. We run up to 1,000 rows through general converter and then through process_entry. If more than 90% of them pass, the dataset is used as it is. Otherwise, the agent writes fix. This way the agent only spends effort on datasets that need it. Finding the cause. For datasets that fail, the agent looks at raw rows, passed rows, failed rows, and the error messages returned by process_entry, grouped by type. From these, it works out what went wrong, for example an unfamiliar tool format, tool inputs stored as text, reasoning kept in different field, or an agent run that was never finished. Writing fix for each dataset. Each fix is small piece of code for one dataset only, with its own tests. It runs before process_entry and converts the data into the form the validator expects. Common fixes move existing reasoning into the expected field, convert tool descriptions and tool outputs to our format, rebuild conversations from logged events, or remove leftover messages from the original agent setup. fix may never make up questions, reasoning, answers, or final replies. Testing the fix again. After each fix, the same rows are checked again with process_entry. The agent gets at most three attempts and stops earlier if the only way forward would be to invent missing content. Datasets that still do not pass are left out. Running on the full dataset and saving the output. The final fix is run on the whole dataset using many CPU workers or cluster jobs, with the same version, validator, and settings as in testing. When results from several jobs are joined, we check that every source row was processed exactly once. For each dataset, configuration, and split, we save the accepted conversations, sample of rejected rows, and summary with exact counts and settings. Keeping record of common problems. Problems we have confirmed are written down with the dataset, counts, cause, and whether they were fixed. Later runs can then recognize known problem instead of investigating it again. Validation. Every converted example must pass process_entry (5.17). For each dataset, the caller chooses few settings, such as whether reasoning is required, the reasoning level, whether some failed tool calls may be tolerated, and the bulk runner saves these settings in each outputs summary. Our team rule is that the agent may not change the validators rules without explicit human approval, so failing dataset must be fixed in its own preprocessing code and not by loosening the checks. process_entry records token counts but does not enforce length limit. Public sources. We processed 30 public datasets from Hugging Face with this workflow, listed in Table 27. Each dataset is cited through its paper when its dataset card gives one, and otherwise through its Hugging Face page. The sources cover math and logic, general chat and instruction following, multiple languages, safety, finance, science, code, software engineering, agent and terminal tasks, and reasoning traces distilled from larger model. Each dataset, configuration, and split was processed and saved separately. In addition to these public SFT datasets, we collected coding RL tasks, summarized in Table 26. sections.title:
5.19 Chat template
We designed the chat template to improve the diversity and efficiency of tool-use training. Rather than
training on a single fixed convention, we exposed the model to multiple tool presentation and tool calling
formats. Tool definitions were represented using JSON, XML, and Markdown, while tool calls used
JSON, XML, and typed XML. Three variations for tool definitions and tool calling produced a total of
nine configurations that we varied during mid-training with a bias towards XML and Markdown tool
presentation (40% each) and XML tool calling (50%) formats. This variation encourages the model to
learn the underlying semantics of tool understanding and selection rather than overfitting to a particular
syntax. For inference, we ultimately selected Markdown as the default tool presentation format because it
was approximately 18.5% more token-efficient than the conventional JSON formatting on our data (see
Figure 37).
sections.content: 88 Figure 37: Token cost of the three tool presentation formats. (a) Average size of the rendered tool block per sample. On our data (771K samples with tools, 249K unique toolsets), Markdown uses 18.5% fewer tokens than JSON and XML 15.2% fewer. The savings are similar or larger on BFCL and τ 2-bench toolsets. (b) Per-tool savings over the 747K unique tools in our data, grouped by the tools size in JSON. Markdown is shorter than JSON for 99.5% of tool uses. Small tools save the most (up to 48%), because JSON syntax makes up larger share of them. Tools over 1K tokens save only about 7%. All averages are weighted by how often each tool or toolset occurs. One of the harder problems we encountered in this seemingly easy endeavor was ensuring that these different presentations exposed the information needed to use each tool. Early versions of our compact renderers omitted or distorted information from the JSON tool definitions, such as union schemas and fields behind local schema references. For example, the passenger argument of an airline-reservation tool referenced shared definition, but the compact presentation never showed that definitions fields. In the resulting traces, the model sometimes supplied date_of_birth where the tool required dob, triggering validation errors and retries. In one of our evaluation runs, fixing this simple bug increased BFCL single-turn accuracy from 74.65% to 76.98% across six presentation/call configurations. (cid:17) The tokens we saved became code we had to maintain Moving beyond raw JSON shifted complexity into the chat template. References, types, and literal values all needed explicit handling, and mistakes could surface as apparent model failures. On our journey of diversifying tool presentation and calling formats, we ended up building small compiler. We settled on Markdown tool presentation that uses 18.5% fewer tokens, but the larger lesson is how varied real-world tool definitions are, and how much code it takes to render all of them faithfully.

sections.title:
6 Post-Training
After the mid-training stages dedicated to seeding broad model capabilities such as handling longer
context and agentic tool use, we turned to post-training. Instead of a fixed stage of training, we think of
post-training as a process of eliciting, refining and adding model capabilities to meet a rapidly evolving
landscape of LLM applications. RL, SFT, and evaluation are tools used flexibly in this process to produce
release-ready checkpoints; community feedback on each release then restarts the cycle. This post-training
iteration further served as a learning process of building the full post-training stack for agentic LLMs. This
section is aimed at sharing these lessons with the community, particularly with new teams taking up the
challenge of building agentic LLMs.
sections.content: 89 We adopted expert training with weight merging instead of mixed-domain training as our RL strategy for the following reasons: major advantage of mixed-domain RL is that abilities gained in one domain can be immediately utilized across other domains, speeding up overall capability improvement. But the same potential has flip side in unique algorithmic challenges that expert training does not have. Unbalanced learning signals can lead to rapid improvement in some domains at the cost of others, and failure modes arising in one domain can quickly propagate to others. Instead of spending time on stabilizing mixed-domain RL, we decided to focus on domain-specific experts for our first agentic post-training iteration. This gave us the opportunity to better understand the data and training behavior for each domain, preparing us for future work on mixed-domain training. Expert training is highly flexible from logistics and organizational perspective. Training domain expert requires fewer computational resources, and different domain experts can be trained by different teams on different clusters, using algorithmic settings and ingredients that can be tuned to each domain independently. Weight merging with recent algorithmic techniques is extremely fast (taking just few minutes) and produces excellent results when used carefully, as we demonstrate for the first time at the multi-hundred-billion parameter scale, in Section 6.4. new version of our RL infrastructure was developed from the ground up in parallel during mid-training, to support long-horizon agentic RL across several domains. Expert RL started after the last stage of mid-training for five domains of expertise we target: search, knowledge work, tool use, scientific reasoning, and instruction following. Following the RL stage, we conducted extensive evaluations to understand gaps in model performance, and continued with round of SFT targeted at closing the identified gaps.

sections.title:
6.1 RL Infrastructure
Long-horizon agentic workloads introduce significant overhead beyond model inference. In our early stack,
rollout throughput was often limited not by GPU serving capacity, but by CPU-side coordination: session
management, tokenization, trajectory assembly, and sandbox orchestration were serialized across a small
number of event loops. This left available inference capacity underutilized as the number of concurrent
trajectories increased.
sections.content: RL360 addresses this bottleneck by decoupling rollout orchestration from training and allowing each component to scale independently. As illustrated in Figure 38, Miles (Chen et al., 2026b) manages rollout collection and policy optimization, Harbor (Harbor Framework Team, 2026) handles agent execution and task environments, SMG22 routes inference requests to SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024), and Megatron-LM (Shoeybi et al., 2019) handles distributed training and policy weight synchronization. The complete implementation, pinned component versions, and reference training recipe are available in the public RL360 repository (IFM, 2026). Scaling the rollout control plane. At high concurrency, the bottleneck shifts from inference to the control plane that launches trials, tracks sessions, and assembles trajectories; our initial setup saturated at 1024 concurrent trajectories. Harbor runs multiple worker processes behind lightweight router that dispatches trials and aggregates worker health and crash diagnostics. Distributing trials exposed two issues: worker-local sample identifiers could collide, and cancellation reached only one worker. We use globally unique sample identifiers and broadcast cancellations to all workers, which also release the cancelled trials session state. 22https://github.com/smg-project/smg 90 Figure 38: RL360 architecture. The rollout, sandbox, inference, and training layers communicate through explicit service boundaries and can be scaled independently. Miles collects trajectories and rewards, Harbor executes agents in task environments, SMG routes inference requests to SGLang, and Megatron-LM updates the policy. Miles shards sessions across multiple session-server backends, pinning each session to one backend that owns its turn-ordered state. All backends share one inference-engine pool, so session handling and inference scale independently. Per-backend concurrency limits, timeouts, and retries with backoff confine slow or failed request to its own trajectory; trajectories that exhaust their retries are dropped. We move trajectory assembly from the central rollout manager into distributed Ray session actors. Each actor merges trajectorys turns into single trainer-ready sample and discards provider and decoding metadata, so the manager receives one compact object per trajectory instead of every turn, and its CPU, memory, and serialization costs no longer grow with the number of in-flight fragments. To avoid request burst when large batch starts, we admit rollouts in waves, bounding peak load on session servers and environment backends without changing the batch size. Trajectory lifecycle and artifacts. Each trajectory carries its global Miles sample index through Harbor, so artifacts written by different workers (trajectory files, object-store paths, dashboard records) cannot collide. At rollout boundaries, Miles issues coordinated abort that Harbors router forwards to every worker, which cancels active trials through Harbors native cancellation path and tears down their environments. Batch transitions therefore have an explicit lifecycle rather than relying on timeouts or process termination for cleanup. We keep the archival record separate from the training data path. Token IDs and log-probabilities reach the trainer through Miles, so Harbors ATIF record retains only what is needed to inspect agent behavior: messages, tool calls, reasoning (stored separately from visible assistant content), and compact usage and cost statistics. Raw provider responses, parser state, and router payloads are dropped, reducing rollout-node memory, serialization, and storage traffic. Malformed tool calls are recorded with explicit failure metadata rather than silently discarded, so format errors stay visible in analysis. Failure-aware batch construction. An infrastructure failure is not policy outcome, and scoring it as zero reward corrupts the learning signal. When other group members succeed, it yields spurious negative advantages; when none do, solvable prompt looks unsolved. We therefore classify rollout outcomes by exit status before dynamic sampling (Yu et al., 2026). group enters the batch only if none of its members failed and its rewards are not all identical. We drop the whole group rather than only its failed members because failures correlate with trajectory behavior (e.g., long or tool-heavy episodes), so the surviving members would yield biased baseline. Truncation at the token or context limit, by contrast, is an outcome of the policy. truncated samples reward still counts toward the groups mean and standard deviation, but its loss is masked, as in overlong filtering (Yu et al., 2026), so the policy is not penalized for exhausting its budget. Malformed tool calls are policy errors rather than failures, so they enter through the reward: Harbor applies configurable penalty either to every affected trajectory or only to those that otherwise succeed. Future Design Goals for Scalable RL Framework. The bottlenecks faced during the RL training of K2-Horizon motivate the following goals for our next-generation RL training system: 1. Isolate failures. An inference engine, environment worker, verifier, rollout service, or trainer should be able to fail and recover independently. 2. Remain distributed end to end. Eliminate the single rollout-manager bottleneck by distributing collection, trajectory assembly, filtering, and verification across actors. 3. Schedule work dynamically. Replace static assignment with cluster-wide scheduling and work redistribution to prevent idle workers and long-tail stragglers. 4. Balance compute and memory. Account for sequence length, inference cost, environment cost, verifier latency, and memory pressurenot only task or token counts. 5. Support very large batches. Handle rollout batches of at least 10,000 samples through streaming, bounded queues, admission control, and backpressure. 6. Minimize data movement. Process data near its producer and transfer only compact, trainer-ready samples or references. 7. Keep the core minimal and extensible. Provide stable mechanisms while leaving rollout, scheduling, filtering, reward, and failure-policy decisions to users. 8. Make behavior observable. Connect tasks, sessions, inference requests, rewards, failures, and training updates through structured logs and stable identifiers. 9. Strengthen verification. Support scalable programmatic and LLM-based task-specific verifiers without placing them on the inference critical path. 10. Support installed agents directly. Run existing agent harnesses through their native interfaces and reconstruct token-faithful training trajectories from their model interactions. Sandboxing. We developed simple sandboxing system using AWS to support agentic RL, with sandboxes as Kubernetes containers on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS). Requests for the sandboxes are handled by server deployment on the same EKS cluster. Task images are stored on Amazon Elastic 92 Container Registry (ECR), using default Kubernetes behavior for caching. Sandbox containers had small nominal memory and vCPU requests, and limits were set to what the RL trainer requested. This enables us to over-pack sandboxes to reduce costs: as long as the sandboxes use bursts of resources at different times, they still get the full resources requested. Egress is handled via an egress proxy deployment on the cluster, with pull-through caches for PyPI, Hugging Face and GitHub. Key challenges and lessons learned: Lazy image loading with Seekable Open Container Initiative (SOCI) was not functional in time. For stability, we disabled SOCI entirely. AWS default Container Network Interface (CNI) was bottleneck for sandbox creation at high churn rates. Sandboxes would be stuck in creation waiting for the CNI to receive new IPs to allocate. This was the primary limiting factor for scaling up the sandbox infrastructure. Gains from collocating rollouts that use the same image are workload dependent. For example, for 1step asynchronous RL with 32 rollouts per task and 4000 total sandboxes, collocating based on images removed all bottlenecks with sandbox creation. For data generation workloads, it pathologically concentrated all of the resource heavy sandboxes onto few nodes. To allow for more GitHub API calls for the entire sandbox cluster, we injected GitHub application token into the sandboxes. This let the sandboxes use authenticated GitHub API rate limits. However, due to an oversight, this token initially allowed access to our private repositories, allowing agents to find task solutions in our dataset repositories. Because of how Kubernetes disk and memory limits are implemented, sandboxes that exceeded their requested amount would be evicted and destroyed. Such infrastructure errors needed to be handled gracefully by the RL trainer. generates group of trajectories, {oi}G

The loss of each trajectory is averaged over the number of tokens Ti before the trajectories are averaged, ensuring every trajectory contributes equally to the gradient q, oi,<t)/πθrollout(oi,t 93 regardless of its length23 and preventing long multi-turn episode from dominating the update over short one. Asynchronous Training. We use non-colocated training where rollouts are generated by separate inference fleet that runs concurrently with the trainer and receives new weights after each update. In the one-step asynchronous training regime, the fleet generates batch using πk+1 while the trainer updates use policy πk and pauses at batch boundary, so every trajectory is at most one policy version stale. For agentic tasks having long, multi-turn trajectories with high variance in trajectory lengths, pausing at batch boundaries (as done in the one-step asynchronous training regime) leaves the fleet idle while the longest trajectories finish, making the rollout phase dominate wall-clock time. We train experts on agentic tasks fully asynchronously, where generations are never paused and finished trajectories are batched as they arrive. This keeps the inference fleet saturated and substantially raises end-to-end throughput, at the cost of increasing staleness; ρi,t absorbs the off-policy gap. We enforce maximum staleness of 5 and trajectories where any token is generated by policy with larger staleness are dropped from the training batch. In the fully asynchronous regime, weight push arrives while trajectory generations are in flight. Rather than discarding these, we use partial rollouts: push interrupts each in-flight trajectory at the request level, i.e. at the boundary of the current model call, while its environment state (sandbox, tool session, user-simulator context) is preserved. Once the new weights are loaded, the episode resumes under the updated policy. Such updates lead to different parts of trajectory being generated by different policies. Since ρi,t is defined per token against the policy that actually generated that token, such mixed-policy trajectories are handled by the same correction, and no environment work is wasted at weight update. Training Hyperparameters. Each expert training (described in Section 6.3 below) uses slightly different setup of hyperparameters for training. The knobs we experiment with are: Rollouts: Context length and global batch size24. All experiments set temperature 1.0 and top-p as 1.0 for rollouts. Optimization: For all experts, we use default Adam optimizer and no KL regularization. Learning rates are tuned for different experts along with weight decay rules. We use gradient-norm clipping throughout and constant learning rate (optionally experimenting with warm-up schedules). Dynamic sampling: Following DAPO (Yu et al., 2026), we use dynamic sampling to filter out groups with all correct and all incorrect trajectories, and use oversampling to maintain batch size across training updates. Asynchronous training: we experiment with asynchronous training with staleness one (i.e., πθtrainer differ by one update) for some experts and fully asynchronous training for other experts. and πθrollout We use truncated importance sampling with ratio cap of 2.0 to control for off-policyness. Reward shaping and entropy regularization: For agentic expert training, we apply penalties to trajectories with malformed, hallucinated (unknown) and/or repeated tool calls. For some experts  (Table 29)  , we add an entropy bonus to prevent mode collapse.
